entry.title: Deploying a CAP app with Fiori app standalone (HTML5 Repo Host)
entry.content:
Typically, a CAP app with a Fiori frontend is deployed using SAP Workzone or Launchpad. You just need to run "cds add portal" or "cds add workzone" to extend the configuration and deploy the app to Cloud Foundry (Deploy to Cloud Foundry | capire). The application will then be listed in the HTML5 tab of your subaccount. However, this approach is only applicable if you are subscribed to SAP Workzone or Launchpad (see below). A few months ago I was asked how to deploy a standalone CAP application with UI. Here is a step-by-step guide to deploying a CAP app with frontend.

There are at least two different approaches. The first exposes the frontend application through the approuter. The other exposes the frontend application to the HTML5 Repo Host (SAP Discovery Center Service - HTML5 Application Repository Service). This has several advantages over the approuter:

  • Zero Down-Time Enablement, the frontend application is decoupled from the application router, meaning that content updates do not require a restart of the application router.
  • The service supports versioning and permissions.
  • Improved availability and performance.

 

How to deploy a Fiori-CAP app to the html5-repo-host:

For simplicity, we will set up a new tiny bookshop example. Based on this backend, we will generate a simple Fiori List Page app.

cds init bookshop --add tiny-sample
cd bookshop

Run the commands below to add some features. We will extend the configuration of the components later.

cds add hana,html5-repo,approuter,mta
cds add xsuaa --for production

Now we are ready to add a Fiori List Report application. Right click on the mta.yaml and select 'Create MTA Module from Template'. The App Wizard will open and you will be able to configure a new Fiori app.

To make the html5 application accessible through the app router, we need to make some changes to its configuration. Locate the router configuration in the “app/router” folder.  Add the “welcomeFile” and “authenticationMethod” properties to the xs-app file. In general, you can add a path to a file or the name of a Fiori app as a welcome file. The app router will redirect the user if accessing the app router. We need to add the name of the Fiori app as "welcomeFile" property. If you have defined a namespace when building the frontend app, make sure you include the namespace without delimiter. After deployment, the app router configuration below will redirect you to the Fiori app.

{
  "welcomeFile": "<Fiori app name>",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "target": "$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "csrfProtection": true
    }
  ]
}

Next, we need to extend the xs-app.json of the Fiori app itself. Add a new route for the odata service to make your cap service accessible from the Fiori app. Add the following snippet to the routes array before the html5-repo route.

{
   "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
   "target": "/odata/$1",
   "destination": "srv-api",
   "csrfProtection": true
}

The app router applies the routes in the order given in the routes array, i.e. if the first route matches, the others are ignored. The target is the service name defined in mta.yaml. The xs-app.json should now look similar to this one.

{
  "welcomeFile": "/index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/resources/(.*)$",
      "target": "/resources/$1",
      "authenticationType": "none",
      "destination": "ui5"
    },
    {
      "source": "^/test-resources/(.*)$",
      "target": "/test-resources/$1",
      "authenticationType": "none",
      "destination": "ui5"
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "csrfProtection": true
    },
    {
      "source": "^(.*)$",
      "target": "$1",
      "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa"
    }
  ]
}

Now we need to add the requires section below to the Fiori app's mta.yaml configuration. This snippet defines the service binding of the frontend app to the CAP service.

 - name: books
  type: html5
  path: app/books
  build-parameters:
    build-result: dist
    builder: custom
    commands:
    - npm install
    - npm run build:cf
    supported-platforms: []
  requires:
  - name: srv-api
    group: destinations
    properties:
      forwardAuthToken: true
      name: srv-api
      url: ~{srv-url}

If you are deploying to a BTP trial account, add the following snippet to the xs-security in the cap root folder. Make sure the link matches the cf api url for your environment.

"oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": ["https://*.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
  }

Add the environment variable "COOKIE_BACKWARD_COMPATIBILITY" to the “app/router/default-env.json” file. The app asked me to add this configuration. For more information, see the app router documentation (@sap/approuter - npm).

{
  "destinations": [
    {
      "name": "srv-api",
      "url": "http://localhost:4004",
      "forwardAuthToken": true
    }
  ],
  "COOKIE_BACKWARD_COMPATIBILITY": true
}

We are all almost done! Install the dependencies, build the CAP app and deploy to Cloud Foundry.

npm i
mbt build
cf deploy …. (or context menu of the mta_archive)

After successfully deploying the application, retrieve the URL using the html5 cf plugin. Run the terminal command below. Add the app name (with namespace) and "index.html" to the URL to open the Fiori app.

cf html5-list -a <app name>-srv -u

Alternatively, navigate to the subaccount in the BTP Cockpit, access your app router and follow the application route. The router will redirect you to the Fiori app.  

Find the app router on the application tab.

Follow the application route and access the fiori app.

 

Further information:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jbq6zaKEUyY

entry.title: Introducing Application Frontend Service
entry.content:
As part of our exciting  SAP Build release, we're happy to announce the release of Application Frontend service, a new SaaS application on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) for hosting, serving and operating frontend applications.

Next Generation Solution for hosting frontend applications

Application Frontend serves as a single point of entry for hosting, serving and operating frontend applications. By consolidating all aspects of UI application management under one managed service, Application Frontend simplifies the development experience and enhances custom application operations.

Bridging the Gap Between Neo and Multi-Cloud

If you have been around SAP BTP for more than 10 years then, most likely, you have used the Neo environment. If you developed an HTML5 application in Neo, then you probably used the HTML5 Runtime. Many customers we met in the past years have reported that the snappy experience they had in Neo, when developing and operating HTML5 applications, was lost when moving to the multi-cloud environment, where the HTML5 Application Repository and the managed application router (approuter) are used.
This feedback was received, noted and motivated us to come up with a new solution for managing HTML5 applications. A solution that will bring back the simplicity and flexibility customers liked so much in the Neo environment. With Application Frontend, we aim to bring that experience into the multi-cloud environment.

The first capabilities Neo fans will find familiar are host-based routing, the versioning concept and a direct deployment option. Additional capabilities like extended control from the SAP BTP cockpit will be added in the future.

But don’t get me wrong, Application Frontend is not a replica of HTML5 Runtime in Neo. It is a multi-cloud service compatible with the multi-cloud development model. We use the same descriptors used in HTML5 Repository and application router, ensuring that developers don't need to learn yet another paradigm.

Very high level architecture diagram

 

A New SaaS application

Application Frontend is a SaaS application which is not coupled to any specific SAP BTP runtime environment or other SAP BTP applications. You can find and subscribe to the service from the SAP BTP cockpit. Application Frontend is also equipped with a service broker to support interaction flows using service instances, for example when using MTA deploy in the CF environment. 

While there is native support in the good old MTA concept for lifecycle management, Application Frontend also provides a command line interface (CLI) as a first-class tool for managing your applications. With the CLI, you can directly interact with the service and execute all actions supported by Application Frontend to enjoy fast response times and new integration opportunities.

 

Supported Use cases

At the moment, Application Frontend supports hosting of single tenant, stand-alone applications. (Stand-alone means applications that are not embedding other applications.)
In the future we will extend the supported use cases to cover more scenarios like applications dependencies, multi-tenancy, native SAP Build Work Zone integration, etc.
Application Frontend is perfect if you have a Build license and developing new HTML5 applications or migrating existing ones from Neo.
If the HTML5 Repository and application router are more suitable for your needs, please continue using them.

Application Frontend management UI in SAP BTP Cockpit

 Next steps

Application Frontend service is starting its journey. We will continuously release additional features to support new scenarios and delight your experience.
In few weeks’ time, we will also make Application Frontend available in the SAP trial environment, so you can try it out more easily.
Note: Application Frontend will reside next to the HTML5 Repository, and the managed Application Router (approuter) hosted in SAP Build Work Zone. Both services will continue to be available, supported and developed as needed.   

 How to get started

SAP Build is available for subscription, more details in SAP Discovery Center
Once you purchased SAP Build, follow these steps for Application Frontend on-boarding.
Check out this intro tutorial for Simple UI Applications with Application Frontend Service

entry.title: Simple UI Applications with Application Frontend Service
entry.content:
In the ever-evolving world of web UI applications, managed SaaS solutions are the preferred choice for hosting and serving UI applications. They offer efficiency and cost-effectiveness. SAP BTP provides robust solutions for UI applications from the early days of its cloud. The latest offering, Application Frontend service, combines the best legacy features with new advancements in technology and infrastructure. In this post I’ll share with you how to get started with Application Frontend service using the CLI, but MTA and API are supported as well.

Prerequisites

To proceed with this tutorial and try everything on your own, you’ll need a few things

  • An SAP BTP subaccount, where you have administrator privileges, with
    • An entitlement to use the “build-default” of Application Frontend service
    • Trust with SAP Cloud Identity tenant
  • Node.js v22.6.0 or later installed on your development environment
  • Application Frontend service CLI tool—afctl

To install the afctl, run

npm install -g @sap/appfront-cli

Setup

To start working with Application Frontend service, you need to subscribe to it and grant yourself the permissions to use it.

  1. In the SAP BTP cockpit, in the subaccount, go to Services > Instances and Subscriptions. Then create a subscription the “build-default” of Application Frontend service.
  2. In the subaccount, go to Security > Role Collections. Then create a role collection (for example, Application Frontend Developer). Open the newly created role collection and add yourself as a user. Make sure the user is from an “application users” identity provider. Add the “Application_Frontend_Developer” role to the role collection and save.

Development & Deployment

Let’s develop an application that prints “Hello, <NAME>!”, where the <NAME> is the first name of the logged-in user. We’ll use Application Frontend’s built-in current user REST API, which returns the attributes of the logged-in user as JSON.

Application Frontend service is agnostic to the tools, development model, and UI frameworks that are used to develop UI applications. However, some application configuration files are required:

The manifest.json file should, at a minimum, declare application name and version in the following format:

{
    "sap.app": {
        "id": "hello",
        "applicationVersion": {
            "version": "1.0.0"
        }
    }
}

The xs-app.json file, where the desired web server features, such as, the routing, the welcome file and authentication are configured. Some features, for example the authentication are enabled by default, and you have an option to switch them off in this file:

{
    "welcomeFile": "/index.html",
    "routes": [{
        "source": "^/user-api/currentUser$",
        "service": "sap-approuter-userapi"
    }, {
        "source": ".*",
        "service": "app-front"
    }]
}

With this example we configure 3 things:

  • If no specific path to the resource is present in the URL, send a redirect to /index.html
  • When the URL path is exactly /user-api/currentUser, send the JSON response with logged-in user attributes
  • For any other URL path, use the URL path as path to the static resource within deployed application

The index.html file would be the following:

<html>
<head>
    <style>
        body {
            display: grid;
            place-content: center;
            position: absolute;
            inset: 0;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Loading...</h1>
    <script>
        fetch(
            './user-api/currentUser', 
            {credentials: 'include'}
        )
        .then(res => res.json())
        .then(user => {
            const h1 = document.querySelector('h1');
            h1.textContent = `Hello, ${user.firstname}!`;
        });
    </script>
</body>
</html>

To deploy the application, use afctl. The first thing, you need to do is to log in:

afctl login --sso -a <api_endpoint>

You can grab the <api_endpoint> from the Application Frontend service landing page. To open it, in the subaccount in the SAP BTP Cockpit, go to Services > Instances and Subscriptions, and click on the Application Frontend service link.

Now, let’s open the terminal in the root folder of our application containing these 3 files and deploy UI application, using afctl:

afctl push

After a few seconds, you should see the runtime URL of deployed application.

Open the link in the browser, log in with your SAP Cloud Identity (if you are not already logged in) and you’ll see “Hello, <NAME>!”, where <NAME> is the first name of the logged in user, in the middle of the web page.

That’s it! Very simple. No mess with infrastructure, servers, certificates, etc. Developing and deploying subsequent applications will be even simpler, since you already have everything set up.

What’s Next

In this post we covered only the very basics of Application Frontend service. In the upcoming posts from the series, we’ll take a look at more advanced Application Frontend capabilities, including:

  • Accessing back-end systems
  • Setting up authorization
  • Securing UI application (CSRF, click-jacking, verb tampering, CSP, CORS)
  • Developing and deploying full-stack applications (MTA)
  • Managing application versions
  • Local preview
  • Integration with SAP BTP services and tools (SAP BTP cockpit, Business Application Studio, SAP Build Work Zone, SAP Fiori tools)

Stay tuned to learn more about what Application Frontend service has to offer already now and the future features to come. Happy coding!

entry.title: Fiori App Deployment in SAP BTP: Why Your App isn't where You think it is
entry.content:
Fiori App Deployment in SAP BTP: Why Your App Isn't Where You Think It Is

When you're delving into SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), especially with a trial account, every successful deployment feels like a mini victory. You build a Fiori app in SAP Business Application Studio (BAS), connect it to a data source (like the SAP Gateway Demo System), deploy it to BTP, and then confidently embed it into SAP Build Work Zone. Success!

But then, you decide to level up your DevOps game by configuring Cloud Transport Management Service (CTMS). The goal: to understand how your precious Fiori app will move from a "development" environment to "QA" and "production" spaces. Naturally, you'd want to see your app residing in your initial "DEV" Cloud Foundry space to confirm its source.

This is where my recent learning journey took an interesting turn, and it's a confusion I want to clarify for others.

My "Where's My App?" Moment

After deploying my Fiori app, my logical next step was to go to the BTP Cockpit, navigate to my subaccount, select Cloud Foundry > Spaces, click into my "dev" space, and then look under Applications.

To my surprise, my Fiori app wasn't listed there! Panic. Did the deployment fail? Is it invisible? Yet, I could still access it perfectly fine from the HTML5 Applications section in the BTP Cockpit and, more importantly, it was fully functional within SAP Build Work Zone.

This discrepancy sparked a deep dive into how Fiori apps are truly deployed on BTP.

CHECK the BTP Deployment Model for Fiori Apps

The key to understanding this lies in the specialized nature of HTML5/UI5 application deployment on the Cloud Foundry environment within BTP.

When you deploy a Fiori/UI5 application from SAP BAS:

  1. It's Not a Standalone Cloud Foundry Application (Usually): Unlike a typical backend service (e.g., a Node.js or Java application) that directly consumes Cloud Foundry resources and appears under "Applications" in a space, your Fiori app's static UI content (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, images) is usually not deployed as an independent Cloud Foundry application instance.

  2. Enter the HTML5 Application Repository: Instead, your Fiori app's static content is deployed to the HTML5 Application Repository service. Think of this as a highly optimized, dedicated storage and serving mechanism specifically for front-end web applications. It's designed for efficient content delivery.

  3. The Approuter's Role: Your Fiori project likely includes an approuter module (or leverages a managed approuter service). The approuter is a Cloud Foundry application instance that you will see listed in your space under Cloud Foundry --> Spaces --> space > Applications. This approuter acts as the single-entry point for your Fiori application. It handles:

    • Authentication (often via XSUAA).

    • Routing requests to your Fiori UI content (which is in the HTML5 Application Repository).

    • Routing requests to any backend services your Fiori app consumes.

So, while the approuter is a visible Cloud Foundry application, your actual Fiori UI content lives in the HTML5 Application Repository, which is a service backing the HTML5 Applications view in the BTP Cockpit.

Checking Fiori App's True "Home"

To truly visualize where your deployed Fiori app content resides, you need to check the HTML5 Applications section:

  1. Log in to your SAP BTP Cockpit.

  2. Navigate to your Subaccount.

  3. In the left-hand navigation, click on HTML5 Applications.

  4. Here, you'll see a list of all your deployed HTML5 applications. Look for your Fiori app by its name.

  5. Crucially, observe the "Space" column for your Fiori app. You should see your initial "dev" space listed there.

if you are unable to see, click on settings icon and add the space column there, by default it's not there

 

This confirms that your Fiori app's deployed content is indeed correctly placed within the HTML5 Application Repository associated with your dev space.

Points to Remember:

  • Fiori/UI5 apps are primarily deployed to the HTML5 Application Repository, not as direct Cloud Foundry application instances. The  approuter is the Cloud Foundry application that serves them.

  • The HTML Applications section in the BTP Cockpit is your go-to place to monitor and confirm the deployment space of your Fiori apps.

Host, serve, and manage frontend applications to extend SAP business solutions.

Application Frontend service lets you host and serve frontend applications. It serves as a single entry point for hosting web-based UI applications to extend SAP's business solutions. The service provides tools for deploying and managing applications, serving static resources, routing backend calls to defined targets, and observability tools.

Application Frontend service is included in the SAP Build.

Application Frontend service supports various channels for managing applications, such as the commonly used Generic Application Content Deployer (GACD) for multitarget applications (MTA), a dedicated UI in the cockpit, and a CLI. These options allow you to choose the channel that best suits your needs.

You can find and subscribe to the service from the SAP BTP cockpit. Application Frontend is also equipped with a service broker to support interaction flows using service instances, for example when using MTA deploy in the CF environment.

Conclusion

Application Frontend Service is a game-changer for Cloud Foundry users. By simplifying UI development, enhancing scalability, and promoting consistency, AFS empowers developers to create high-quality applications more efficiently. As cloud-native development continues to evolve, integrating tools like AFS will be crucial in staying ahead of the curve and delivering exceptional user experiences.

entry.title: Running a SAPUI5 App from a Previous Commit Without Affecting Remote Repository
entry.content:
Introduction

          Ever needed to test or run your SAPUI5 application from an earlier commit without disturbing your current branch or affecting the remote repository? Whether it's for debugging, rollback testing, or feature validation, Git provides a safe and clean way to do this — using detached HEAD state and local branches. Here's a step-by-step guide to achieve just that.

 

Step-by-Step: Run an Older Version of Your SAPUI5 App Safely

Step 1: View Commit History

To identify which commit you want to revisit:

git log --oneline

This will display recent commits with their short hash and message. Identify the one that's 4 commits back or use:

git checkout HEAD~4

 

Step 2: Checkout the Older Commit

git checkout <commit-hash>

Or for 4 commits ago:

git checkout HEAD~4

This moves you into a detached HEAD state, a safe mode where changes don’t impact your current branch.

 

Step 3: Run Your SAPUI5 Application

Use your usual development server to run the app:

ui5 serve

or

npm start

Your app now runs exactly as it existed 4 commits ago.

 

Step 4: (Optional) Create a Local Test Branch

If you want to make edits or test features in that older state:

git checkout -b temp-test-branch

This lets you commit and experiment locally — no impact on the remote repo.

 

Step 5: Return to Your Latest Code

Once done, simply switch back to your latest working branch:

git checkout main

 

Why This Approach is Safe?

- No changes are pushed to the remote.

- The main branch and its history remain intact.

- You can safely test, debug, or demo older versions of your app.

- Great for testing fixes without branching off prematurely.

 

Conclusion

          Testing previous versions of your SAPUI5 app doesn't need to be risky. By using Git's detached HEAD mode and optional local branches, you gain full control without affecting your project's main history or remote repo. It’s a clean, safe, and professional way to revisit and test the past.

 

Thank you for taking the time to read this blog!

If you found this helpful, feel free to share your thoughts, feedback, or questions in the comments! Let's keep learning and growing together. Happy coding!

entry.title: Version Control Made Simple with Application Frontend Service
entry.content:
As developers, we all know that deploying a new version of an application can be both exciting and risky. Whether you’re rolling out a minor UI fix or launching a major redesign, the ability to manage multiple versions with confidence is key to a smooth delivery process.

With Application Frontend Service, version management is built in from the start, letting you deploy, view, roll back, and promote frontend versions directly from the CLI or SAP BTP Cockpit. In this post, we’ll show you how it works and how to make the most of it.

Why Version Management Matters

Application Frontend Service allows you to host and serve UI applications in SAP BTP. But what happens when a bug slips through? Or when you need to test a new version without affecting your end users?

That’s where the versioning concept in Application Frontend Service comes in.

Application Frontend Service supports multiple coexisting versions of the same application, each one deployed independently and maintained separately.
In the manifest.json file of your application, you define the version name using the applicationVersion property. This allows you to deploy multiple versions of the same application, all sharing the same application ID but with different version identifiers.

Every version:

  • Has its dedicated version-specific URL
  • Can reference different services and codebases
  • Can be tested or validated in parallel with the current live version

Each application has exactly one active version at any given time. The active version is served from the application’s main URL. All other versions are accessible only via their version-specific URLs.
The active version is the version that is available to the end users.

When you deploy an application, it becomes the active version by default, served at the application’s main URL. But you can also deploy a version without activating it, test it safely, and switch to it later with a single command.

Real-Life Example: Test and Promote with Zero Downtime

Let’s say you’ve deployed version 0.0.1 of your application, myApp, and it’s running smoothly in production. You’re now working on version 0.0.2 with a few improvements or new features. With Application Frontend Service, you can deploy version 0.0.2 without making it active right away.

Each application in Application Frontend Service is assigned a unique main URL when it is first deployed. For example:

https://myapp-wscfr.eu10.appfront.cloud.sap

This main URL always returns the currently active version of the application.

In addition, each deployed version receives its version-specific URL, such as:

https://myapp-wscfr-v0_0_1.eu10.appfront.cloud.sap
https://myapp-wscfr-v0_0_2.eu10.appfront.cloud.sap

With Application Frontend Service, you can:

  • Deploy version 0.0.2 without activating it
  • Access it directly through its version-specific URL:
    https://myapp-wscfr-v0_0_2.eu10.appfront.cloud.sap
  • Let your testers or internal users try it out
  • Keep version 0.0.1 active and served via the main URL
  • Once validated, promote version 0.0.2 to active, and your main URL: https://myapp-wscfr.eu10.appfront.cloud.sap will now serve the new version to all users

All of this happens without downtime, without breaking the existing deployment, and without overwriting any previously deployed version.

Controlling Activation During Deployment

In the previous example, we saw how useful it is to deploy a new version without activating it right away.
By default, any new deployment to the Application Frontend Service becomes the active version. But if you want to delay activation, for example, to perform internal validation, you can control this behavior in two ways, depending on how you deploy.

When deploying an application using the GACD (Generic Application Content Deployer) module

If you are deploying a multi-target application (MTA), you can prevent automatic activation by setting activateVersion: false under the parameters of the GACD module in your mta.yaml file:

...
  parameters:
    config:
      activateVersion: false
      destinations:
        - name: ui5
          url: https://ui5.sap.com

When deploying with afctl push

If you're using the Application Frontend service CLI to deploy applications, you can achieve the same behavior using one of the following options:

  • Pass the --no-activate (or-n) flag to the afctl push command:
afctl push <path-to-app> -n
  • Or set "activateVersion": false in the configuration file (e.g., conf.json):
{
  "activateVersion": false
}

Note: If both the CLI flag and the configuration file contain activation settings, the CLI flag takes precedence.

For example, the following command uses a configuration file that may contain "activateVersion": true, but the -n flag overrides it and prevents activation:

afctl push <path-to-app> -c conf.json -n

With either method, the new version will be deployed and accessible via its version-specific URL. Still, the application’s main URL will continue to serve the currently active version until you explicitly promote the new one.

Managing Application Versions in SAP BTP Cockpit

To access the Application Frontend UI in SAP BTP Cockpit, your user must be assigned the Application Frontend Viewer role. To activate or delete versions, you need the Application Frontend Developer role.

Viewing Your Applications

  1. In the left-hand navigation bar of the SAP BTP Cockpit, choose HTML5 / Application Frontend.
  2. You'll see a list of applications that have been deployed to the Application Frontend Service in your subaccount.
  3. For each application, you can see its active version.
  4. To open and run an application, you can click either the application name or the active version.
  5. If you choose to delete an application, all of its versions (including the active one) will be permanently deleted.

Viewing and Managing Versions

To see all deployed versions of an application:

  1. Click anywhere on the row of the application.
  2. A detail pane will open on the right, showing all the deployed versions of that application.

Here you can activate versions, delete them, or view logs for a specific version.

To change the active version of an application:

  • Click the Activate version icon on the version you want to promote.
  • The active version indicator will move to that version.

Only one version of an application can be active at a time.

To delete a specific version of an application:

  • Click the Delete icon on the version you want to remove

Note: This action is permanent. Deleted versions cannot be recovered.

Additional Notes

  • You cannot delete an active version. To delete an active version, you must first activate another one.
  • An application can have a maximum of 10 versions. Once this limit is reached, you must delete older versions before deploying new ones.

Let’s see how all of this looks in a real example.

I have deployed an application called “employees.” It currently has a single version, 1.0.0, which was activated by default on deployment.

This is how the application looks:

Note the URL. This is the main URL of the application.

I can also run the same version using its version-specific URL:

Now I want to enhance the application by adding search and sort controls, and I also want to remove the “Employees Overview” title.

After making these changes, I deploy version 2.0.0 of the application using the --no-activate flag, meaning this version will not become active immediately.

At this point, two versions of the application exist:

Since the new version was not activated, the main application URL still serves version 1.0.0 - without the new features:

However, I can access and test version 2.0.0 using its version-specific URL:

The search and sort controls are visible, and everything is working as expected.

Next, I activate version 2.0.0.

Now version 2.0.0 is active.

The main application URL serves the updated version with the new features:

The previous version, 1.0.0, remains available through its version-specific URL, and I can roll back to it if needed:

Managing Application Versions with the Application Frontend Service CLI

You can perform the same version management actions using the Application Frontend service CLI.
To activate or delete versions, you need the Application Frontend Developer role.

Activate a version

To activate a specific version of an application, use:

afctl activate APPLICATION VERSION

Arguments:

  • APPLICATION – Name of the deployed application
  • VERSION – Name of the application version you want to activate

Delete a version

To delete a specific version:

afctl delete APPLICATION VERSION

Caution: If you don't specify an application version, all versions of the application will be deleted. This action cannot be undone.

View all versions
To view versions, your user must be assigned the Application Frontend Viewer role.

To list all deployed versions of an application:

afctl list APPLICATION

For example, if you run afctl list employees after activating version 2.0.0 in the example above, the output would show all available versions, including the active one.

As you can see, with built-in versioning and flexible deployment options, Application Frontend Service makes it easy to deliver updates with confidence.
Whether you work in the SAP BTP Cockpit or prefer the CLI, you can roll out changes safely without impacting the live version during development or testing.

entry.title: SAP CAP Lessons Learned: Reject error message missing on HTML5 Repository app?
entry.content:
Good day fellow CAPpers,

Today I'll share one of the lessons I've learned working with CAP, something that may not be clear in the current tutorials or documentation. When running locally, or even in BTP on a Cloud Foundry-based front end, whenever you reject a request, you would expect that the message appears to the user:

The top bold message is in the front end SAPUI5 app, and the bottom, the description, comes from CAP, in the req.reject call:

try {
  const con = await cds.connect.to('SERVICE_SRV');
  let entry;
  // ...
  const result = await con.run(
    INSERT.into(EntitySet).entries(entry)
   );
} catch (err) {
   req.reject(500, err.message);
}

This executes as expected on CAP, both locally and on BTP. However, in the front end, the message is only displayed locally, not on BTP if the app is deployed on the HTML5 Application Repository:

 This gave me a big headache, especially because a few weeks earlier it was displaying fine, whereas now the message is lost and replaced for "Internal Server Error".

I even debugged remotely the CAP app running on BTP to double check, and the error message was correctly set there, on the req.reject statement.

Finally, I resorted and opened a case (ticket, incident) for SAP. After providing the required test code, they gave me a solution: replace the 500 code for 400.

I chose 500 because out of the HTTP response status codes, 500 is for server errors. Since the error message I wanted to display was on the server side, I opted for 500. But apparently, you should always stick to 400 (client error) to make it work.

SAP failed to provide me an explanation to this behavior of the HTML5 Application Repository, and its behavior is like of a black box, where we can't see what's happening inside.

 

TLDR

Therefore, whenever you want to reject a request in CAP AND send the error message to the user with the details of the error AND you have deployed your app in the HTML5 Repo, use HTTP code 400.

 

May this post help you on your troubleshooting. Reply if you find any issues so I, and the community, can help.

Lucas Magrini Rigo

entry.title: Fullstack CAP Application with HANA Cloud (Decoupled Architecture) [Part-1]
entry.content:
Developing the CAP Application Locally with SQLite

In this blog series, I will walk you through building an Incident Management application using SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) with Node.js, connected to SAP HANA Cloud, and deployed on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry environment.

The frontend is a Fiori Elements application deployed separately to the HTML5 Application Repository — making this a fully decoupled architecture.

Here is what we will cover across this series:

— Develop the CAP application locally using SQLite (this post)
— Connect the CAP app to SAP HANA Cloud
— Deploy the CAP backend to Cloud Foundry
— Build the Fiori Elements UI using SAP Fiori tools
— Configuring Destination in BTP
— Deploy the Fiori app to the HTML5 Application Repository

Before deploying anything to the cloud, it is always a good practice to build and test your CAP application locally. In this part, we will:

- Initialize the CAP project
- Define the domain model (entities)
- Create two OData services (Admin and Processor)
- Add sample data using CSV files
- Run and test the application locally using SQLite as the database

Let's get started!


PREREQUISITES

Make sure the following tools are installed and configured on your machine before proceeding:

- Node.js (v18 or higher recommended)
- @SAP/cds-dk installed globally:

npm install -g @SAP/cds-dk

- VS Code with the SAP CDS Language Support extension (recommended) / Business Application Studio (BAS)
- Basic familiarity with CAP and OData concepts is helpful


STEP 1 — CREATE THE CAP PROJECT

Open a terminal and run the following command to initialize a new CAP project with Node.js support:

cds init --add nodejs incident-management

This creates a new folder called "incident-management" with the standard CAP project structure.

Navigate into the project folder:

cd incident-management

Install the required Node.js dependencies:

npm install

 

After installation, your project structure will look like this:

incident-management/
├── db/ → Domain models (entities, types)
├── srv/ → Service definitions (OData services)
├── app/ → UI applications (used in later parts)
├── package.json
└── .cdsrc.json


STEP 2 — ADD THE DOMAIN MODEL

The domain model defines all the data entities for our application.
Inside the "db" folder, create a new file named: schema.cds

Paste the following code into schema.cds:

using {
  cuid,
  managed,
  sap.common.CodeList
} from '@sap/cds/common';

namespace sap.capire.incidents;

/**
* Incidents created by Customers.
*/
entity Incidents : cuid, managed {
  customer     : Association to Customers;
  title        : String @title: 'Title';
  urgency      : Association to Urgency default 'M';
  status       : Association to Status default 'N';
  conversation : Composition of many {
                   key ID        : UUID;
                       timestamp : type of managed : createdAt;
                       author    : type of managed : createdBy;
                       message   : String;
                 };
}

/**
* Customers entitled to create support Incidents.
*/
entity Customers : managed {
  key ID           : String;
      firstName    : String;
      lastName     : String;
      name         : String = trim(firstName || ' ' || lastName);
      email        : EMailAddress;
      phone        : PhoneNumber;
      incidents    : Association to many Incidents
                       on incidents.customer = $self;
      creditCardNo : String(16) @assert.format: '^[1-9]\d{15}$';
      addresses    : Composition of many Addresses
                       on addresses.customer = $self;
}

entity Addresses : cuid, managed {
  customer      : Association to Customers;
  city          : String;
  postCode      : String;
  streetAddress : String;
}

entity Status : CodeList {
  key code        : String enum {
        new = 'N';
        assigned = 'A';
        in_process = 'I';
        on_hold = 'H';
        resolved = 'R';
        closed = 'C';
      };
      criticality : Integer;
}

entity Urgency : CodeList {
  key code        : String enum {
        high = 'H';
        medium = 'M';
        low = 'L';
      };
      criticality : Integer;
}

type EMailAddress : String;
type PhoneNumber  : String;

The model uses the namespace: sap.capire.incidents

It imports three built-in CDS types from @SAP/cds/common:

- cuid → automatically generates a UUID as the primary key.
- managed → automatically tracks createdAt, createdBy, modifiedAt, modifiedBy.
- CodeList → a base type for value-list entities like Status and Urgency.

Here is a description of each entity defined in the schema:

INCIDENTS
The core entity of the application. Each incident is raised by a Customer and has a title, an urgency level (default: Medium), and a status (default: New). It also contains an inline Composition of conversations — meaning each incident can have multiple conversation/comment entries stored together with it.

CUSTOMERS
Represents the customers who raise incidents. Stores their first name, last name, email, phone, and credit card number. The "name" field is a computed field that automatically combines firstName and lastName. Each customer can have multiple Addresses and multiple Incidents linked to them.

ADDRESSES
Stores the physical address of a customer, including city, postal code, and street address. It is a composition child of Customers.

STATUS
A code list entity representing the lifecycle stages of an incident:
N → New
A → Assigned
I → In Process
H → On Hold
R → Resolved
C → Closed
Each status has a criticality value used for UI color coding in Fiori.

URGENCY
A code list entity representing the priority level of an incident:
H → High
M → Medium
L → Low
Each urgency level also carries a criticality value for UI color coding.


STEP 3 — CREATE THE SERVICES

CAP uses service definitions to expose your entities as OData endpoints.
We will create two separate service files inside the "srv" folder.

a) incidents_admin.cds

This service is used by administrators to manage customers and incidents. It exposes the Customers entity (with OData Draft enabled for edit flows) and the Incidents entity.

The service is published at the path: /odata/v4/incidents-admin

using {sap.capire.incidents as my} from '../db/schema';


/**
 * Service used by administrators to manage customers and incidents.
 */

 @Path: 'incidents-admin'
service AdminService {
    @odata.draft.enabled
    entity Customers as projection on my.Customers;
    entity Incidents as projection on my.Incidents;
}


b) incidents_processor.cds

This service is used by support personnel (incident processors). It exposes the Incidents entity (with OData Draft enabled) as the main working entity. The Customers entity is auto-exposed as a read-only entity — meaning processors can view customer data when working on an incident, but cannot modify it.

The service is published at the path: /odata/v4/incidents-processor

using {sap.capire.incidents as my} from '../db/schema';

/**
 * Service used by support personell, i.e. the incidents' 'processors'.
 */


@path: 'incidents-processor'
service ProcessorService  {
    @odata.draft.enabled
    entity Incidents as projection on my.Incidents;

    // @readonly
    // entity Customers as projection on my.Customers;

    annotate my.Customers with @CDS.autoexpose; // Exposes Customers entity as read only entity
}


> WHY TWO SERVICES?
Separating admin and processor services is a best practice in CAP. It lets you assign different authorization roles to each service and expose only what each user role actually needs. This follows the  principle of least privilege and makes it easier to apply security restrictions later (covered in a future part of this series).


STEP 4 — GENERATE CSV TEMPLATES AND ADD INITIAL DATA

CAP provides a built-in command to auto-generate CSV template files based on your domain model.

Run:

cds add data

This creates empty CSV files inside a newly created "db/data" folder.

The file names follow the pattern: <namespace>-<EntityName>.csv
e.g., sap.capire.incidents-Customers.csv

CAP automatically picks up these files and loads them as seed/initial data every time the application starts in development mode.

Now add the following sample data to each file:

a) db/data/sap.capire.incidents-Addresses.csv
Contains address records for each customer (city, postal code, street).

ID,customer_ID,city,postCode,streetAddress
17e00347-dc7e-4ca9-9c5d-06ccef69f064,1004155,Rome,00164,Piazza Adriana
d8e797d9-6507-4aaa-b43f-5d2301df5135,1004161,Munich,80809,Olympia Park
ff13d2fa-e00f-4ee5-951c-3303f490777b,1004100,Walldorf,69190,Dietmar-Hopp-Allee


b) db/data/sap.capire.incidents-Customers.csv
Contains three sample customers with ID, name, email, and phone.

ID,firstName,lastName,email,phone
1004155,Daniel,Watts,daniel.watts@demo.com,+39-555-123
1004161,Stormy,Weathers,stormy.weathers@demo.com,+49-020-022
1004100,Sunny,Sunshine,sunny.sunshine@demo.com,+49-555-789


c) db/data/sap.capire.incidents-Incidents.conversation.csv
Contains conversation/comment entries linked to incidents via the
"up__ID" foreign key (CAP convention for composition parent).

ID,up__ID,timestamp,author,message
2b23bb4b-4ac7-4a24-ac02-aa10cabd842c,3b23bb4b-4ac7-4a24-ac02-aa10cabd842c,1995-12-17T03:24:00Z,Harry John,Can you please check if battery connections are fine?

9583f982-d7df-4aad-ab26-301d4a157cd7,3583f982-d7df-4aad-ab26-301d4a157cd7,2022-09-04T12:00:00Z,Sunny Sunshine,Please check why the solar panel is broken.

d) db/data/sap.capire.incidents-Incidents.csv
Contains four sample incidents with title, urgency code, status code, and a reference to the customer who raised them.

ID,customer_ID,title,urgency_code,status_code
3b23bb4b-4ac7-4a24-ac02-aa10cabd842c,1004155,Inverter not functional,H,C
3a4ede72-244a-4f5f-8efa-b17e032d01ee,1004161,No current on a sunny day,H,N
3ccf474c-3881-44b7-99fb-59a2a4668418,1004161,Strange noise when switching off Inverter,M,N
3583f982-d7df-4aad-ab26-301d4a157cd7,1004100,Solar panel broken,H,I


e) db/data/sap.capire.incidents-Status.csv
Contains the status code list: N, A, I, H, R, C with descriptions and criticality values.

code,descr,criticality
N,New,0
A,Assigned,0
I,In Process,2
H,On Hold,0
R,Resolved,3
C,Closed,1


f) db/data/sap.capire.incidents-Urgency.csv
Contains the urgency code list: H, M, L with descriptions and criticality values.

code,descr,criticality
H,High,1
M,Medium,2
L,Low,3


STEP 5 — RUN THE PROJECT WITH SQLITE

First, deploy the schema to a local SQLite database file:

cds deploy --to sqlite

Then start the development server with live-reload:

cds watch

Once the server starts, open your browser and go to: http://localhost:4004 in your browser.

You should see the CDS welcome page listing all available OData service endpoints:

 

The two services and their exposed entities will be listed:

/odata/v4/incidents-admin
→ Customers (with Fiori preview)
→ Incidents (with Fiori preview)

/odata/v4/incidents-processor
→ Incidents (with Fiori preview)
→ Customers (with Fiori preview — read-only)

You can click the "Fiori preview" link next to any entity to open an auto-generated Fiori Elements UI — useful for quick testing without building a full UI yet.

You can also directly access the raw OData feed in the browser.

For example: http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/incidents-processor/Incidents

This will return the incident records from your CSV seed data in JSON format, confirming that the data was loaded correctly.

 


SUMMARY

In Part 1, we successfully:

✔ Created a CAP Node.js project using cds init
✔ Defined the domain model with Incidents, Customers, Addresses, Conversations, Status, and Urgency entities
✔ Created two OData services — AdminService and ProcessorService —with appropriate entity exposure for each user role
✔ Added initial seed data using CSV files
✔ Ran and validated the application locally using SQLite

The application is fully functional locally. In Part 2 , we will replace SQLite with SAP HANA Cloud and prepare the project for cloud deployment.

entry.title: Fullstack CAP Application with HANA Cloud (Decoupled Architecture) [Part-2]
entry.content:
Adding CDS Annotations to Build the Fiori UI

In Part 1 , we built and tested our CAP application locally using SQLite. The OData services were working, but when we clicked "Fiori preview" the UI showed raw data with no field labels, no filters, and no meaningful layout.

In this Part, we will add CDS Annotations to shape the Fiori Elements UI —  defining what fields appear, how they are labelled, how the list and detail pages are structured, and which fields get dropdown value helps.

The best part: we do all of this entirely in CDS — no UI5 code needed. Fiori Elements reads these annotations and automatically renders the UI.


WHAT ARE CDS ANNOTATIONS?

CDS Annotations are metadata decorators that you add to your entities or service projections. They tell the Fiori Elements framework how to render the UI — which columns appear in the list, what sections exist on the detail page, which fields should show a value help dropdown, and how labels should read in the browser.

We organize our annotations into three separate files, each focused on one concern:

labels.cds → Human-readable field labels for UI display
layout.cds → Page layout: list columns, detail sections, filters
valuehelps.cds → Dropdown/value help configuration for input fields

Keeping them separate makes the code easier to read and maintain as the application grows.

 

STEP 1 — CREATE THE ANNOTATIONS FOLDER AND FILES

Inside the "app" folder of your CAP project, create a new folder named: annotations

Your folder structure will look like this:

incident-management/
├── app/
│ └── annotations/
│ ├── labels.cds
│ ├── layout.cds
│ └── valuehelps.cds
├── db/
└── srv/

Now create each of the three files with the content below.


a) app/annotations/labels.cds

This file assigns human-readable labels to every field in the Incidents, Customers, Addresses, Status, and Urgency entities. Without these, Fiori Elements falls back to the raw technical field names (e.g., "status_code" instead of "Status").

using {sap.capire.incidents as my} from '../../db/schema';

annotate my.Incidents with @title: 'Incidents' {
    ID           @title          : 'ID';
    createdAt    @title          : 'Created At';
    createdBy    @title          : 'Created By';
    modifiedAt   @title          : 'Modified At';
    modifiedBy   @title          : 'Modified By';
    customer     @title: 'Customer'  : {
        Text           : customer.name,
        TextArrangement: #TextOnly
    };
    title        @title          : 'Title';
    urgency      @title: 'Urgency'   : {
        Text           : urgency.descr,
        TextArrangement: #TextFirst
    };
    status       @title: 'Status'    : {
        Text           : status.descr,
        TextArrangement: #TextFirst
    };
    conversation @title          : 'Conversation';
}

annotate my.Customers {
    ID           @title: 'Customer ID';
    createdAt    @title: 'Created At';
    createdBy    @title: 'Created By';
    modifiedAt   @title: 'Modified At';
    modifiedBy   @title: 'Modified By';
    firstName    @title: 'First Name';
    lastName     @title: 'Last Name';
    name         @title: 'Name';
    email        @title: 'Email';
    phone        @title: 'Phone';
    creditCardNo @title: 'Credit Card No';
    incidents    @title: 'Incidents';
    addresses    @title: 'Addresses';
}

annotate my.Addresses with @title: 'Addresses' {
    customer      @title         : 'Customer';
    city          @title         : 'City';
    postCode      @title         : 'Post Code';
    streetAddress @title         : 'Street Address';
}

annotate my.Status {
    code        @title: 'Status Code'  : {
        Text           : descr,
        TextArrangement: #TextFirst
    };
    criticality @title: 'Criticality';
    descr       @title: 'Status Description';
}

annotate my.Urgency {
    code  @title: 'Urgency Code'  : {
        Text           : descr,
        TextArrangement: #TextFirst
    };
}

b) app/annotations/layout.cds
This file defines the full UI layout for the ProcessorService.Incidents entity. It controls both the List Report page and the Object (detail) page.

using {ProcessorService} from '../../srv/incidents_processor';

annotate ProcessorService.Incidents with : {
    HeaderInfo         : {
        TypeName      : 'Incident',
        TypeNamePlural: 'Incidents',
        Title         : {Value: title},
        Description   : {Value: customer.name}
    },
    Facets             : [
        {
            $Type : 'UI.CollectionFacet',
            Label : 'Overview',
            Facets: [
                {
                    Label : 'General Information',
                    $Type : 'UI.ReferenceFacet',
                    Target: '@UI.FieldGroup#GenInfo',
                },
                {
                    Label : 'Status',
                    $Type : 'UI.ReferenceFacet',
                    Target: '@UI.FieldGroup#Status',
                }
            ],

        },
        {
            $Type : 'UI.ReferenceFacet',
            Label : 'Conversations',
            Target: 'conversation/@UI.LineItem',
        }
    ],

    FieldGroup #Status : {
        Label: 'Details',
        $Type: 'UI.FieldGroupType',
        Data : [
            {
                Value                    : status_code,
                Label                    : 'Status',
                Criticality              : status.criticality,
                CriticalityRepresentation: #WithIcon,
            },
            {
                Value                    : urgency_code,
                Label                    : 'Urgency',
                Criticality              : urgency.criticality,
                CriticalityRepresentation: #WithoutIcon,
            }
        ]
    },

    FieldGroup #GenInfo: {
        Label: 'Overview',
        $Type: 'UI.FieldGroupType',
        Data : [
            {Value: customer.name},
            {Value: title}
        ]
    },

    LineItem           : [
        {
            Value         : title,
            .Importance: #High
        },
        {
            Value         : customer.name,
            .Importance: #High,
        },
        {
            Value                    : status_code,
            Criticality              : status.criticality,
            CriticalityRepresentation: #WithIcon,
            .Importance           : #High,
        },
        {
            Value                    : urgency_code,
            .Importance           : #Low,
            Criticality              : urgency.criticality,
            CriticalityRepresentation: #WithoutIcon,
        },
    ],

    SelectionFields    : [
        customer_ID,
        status_code,
        urgency_code
    ],
};

annotate ProcessorService.Incidents.conversation with : {LineItem: [
    {
        Value: message,
        Label: 'Message'
    },
    {Value: author},
    {Value: timestamp}
], }


c) app/annotations/valuehelps.cds

This file adds dropdown / value help popups to input fields on the Incidents entity, making data entry easier and consistent.

using {ProcessorService} from '../../srv/incidents_processor';

annotate ProcessorService.Incidents with {
    status   .ValueListWithFixedValues;
    urgency  .ValueListWithFixedValues;
    customer .ValueList: {
        CollectionPath: 'Customers',
        Parameters    : [
            {
                $Type            : 'Common.ValueListParameterInOut',
                LocalDataProperty: customer_ID,
                ValueListProperty: 'ID'
            },
            {
                $Type            : 'Common.ValueListParameterDisplayOnly',
                ValueListProperty: 'name',
            },
            {
                $Type            : 'Common.ValueListParameterDisplayOnly',
                ValueListProperty: 'email',
            },
            {
                $Type            : 'Common.ValueListParameterDisplayOnly',
                ValueListProperty: 'phone',
            },
        ]
    }
}


STEP 2 — RUN LOCALLY WITH SQLITE AND PREVIEW THE UI

Now that annotations are in place, re-deploy the schema and restart the server:

cds deploy --to sqlite
cds watch

Open your browser at: http://localhost:4004

You will see the familiar CDS welcome page. This time, click "Fiori preview" next to the "Incidents" entity under the /odata/v4/processor service.

 

The List Report and Object page now renders with full layout and labels.

 

 


SUMMARY

In Part 2, we successfully:

✔ Created an "annotations" folder under app/ with three CDS files
✔ Added field labels for all entities (labels.cds)
✔ Defined the List Report columns, filter bar, Object Page layout and detail page sections (layout.cds)
✔ Configured value help dropdowns for Status, Urgency, and Customer (valuehelps.cds)
✔ Previewed the fully rendered Fiori Elements UI locally with SQLite

In Part 3 , we will set up SAP HANA Cloud on BTP — creating the database instance and mapping it to our Cloud Foundry space.

entry.title: Fullstack CAP Application with HANA Cloud (Decoupled Architecture) [Part-3]
entry.content:
Setting Up SAP HANA Cloud on BTP

In Part 2 , we added CDS Annotations and previewed the Fiori UI locally with SQLite. Now it is time to move to the cloud database layer.

In this Part, we will set up SAP HANA Cloud on SAP BTP so our CAP application can use it as the production database. This involves several one-time BTP configuration steps before we can deploy anything.

Here is what we will do in this part:

1. Verify SAP HANA Cloud is entitled at the Global Account level
2. Assign the HANA Cloud service plans to your Subaccount
3. Subscribe to HANA Cloud Tools via the Service Marketplace
4. Assign the required HANA Cloud roles to your user
5. Create a SAP HANA Cloud database instance
6. Map the Cloud Foundry environment to the HANA Cloud instance

All of these steps are done in the SAP BTP Cockpit and SAP HANA Cloud Central.

STEP 1 — VERIFY HANA CLOUD ENTITLEMENTS IN THE GLOBAL ACCOUNT

Before creating any HANA Cloud resources, confirm that your Global Account has the SAP HANA Cloud service entitlement available.

entry.title: Fullstack CAP Application with HANA Cloud (Decoupled Architecture) [Part-4]
entry.content:
Connecting CAP application to HANA Cloud and Deploying  to Cloud Foundry

In Part 3 , we created the SAP HANA Cloud instance (SHC_DB) on BTP and mapped it to our Cloud Foundry space.

In this Part, we will:

- Update package.json with the correct CDS profiles for each environment
- Run cds add hana to wire the CAP project for HANA Cloud deployment
- Build the MTA archive using mbt build
- Deploy the CAP backend to Cloud Foundry using cf deploy
- Verify the deployment and explore the HANA tables in DB Explorer
- Run the app locally in hybrid mode — connected to the deployed HANA instance

PREREQUISITES

Make sure the following tools are installed before proceeding:

- Cloud Foundry CLI (cf) — logged in to your BTP CF environment: cf login
- MBT (Multi-Target Application Build Tool): npm install -g mbt
- @sap/cds-dk (already installed from Part 1)


STEP 1 — UPDATE PACKAGE.JSON WITH CDS PROFILES

The package.json in the CAP project already has a "cds" section that defines how the app connects to the database in each environment. We need to make sure the three profiles are correctly configured:

development → uses SQLite (local, in-file database — for cds watch)
hybrid → uses SAP HANA Cloud (local app, cloud database — for testing)
production → uses SAP HANA Cloud (fully deployed on CF)

Update or verify the "cds" section in your package.json:

{
  "name": "incident-management",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Incident Management CAP Application",
  "repository": "<Add your repository here>",
  "license": "UNLICENSED",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "@cap-js/hana": "^2",
    "@sap/cds": "^9",
    "@sap/cds-dk": "^9",
    "@sap/xssec": "^4",
    "express": "^5"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@cap-js/sqlite": "^2",
    "@sap/cds-dk": "^9",
    "cds-plugin-ui5": "^0.17.0"
  },
  "cds": {
    "requires": {
      "[development]": {
        "auth": {
          "kind": "dummy"
        },
        "db": {
          "kind": "sqlite"
        }
      },
      "[hybrid]": {
        "auth": {
          "kind": "dummy"
        },
        "db": {
          "kind": "hana-cloud"
        }
      },
      "[production]": {
        "auth": {
          "kind": "dummy"
        },
        "db": {
          "kind": "hana-cloud"
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "scripts": {
    "start": "cds-serve",
    "watch": "cds watch",
    "watch-incidents": "cds watch --open incidents/index.html?sap-ui-xx-viewCache=false --livereload false"
  }
}

WHY THREE PROFILES?
This pattern lets you use the same codebase across all environments without changing any code — just switch the profile.

SQLite keeps local development fast and offline.

Hybrid lets you test against real HANA data without a full CF deployment.

Production is used when the app runs on Cloud Foundry.

 

STEP 2 — RUN cds add hana

Run the following command in the terminal from inside the project folder:

cds add hana

This single command does several important things to prepare your CAP project for SAP HANA Cloud deployment:

- Adds the @cap-js/hana dependency to package.json (HANA database adapter)
- Generates or updates the mta.yaml file with the correct MTA module definitions for CF deployment
- Adds an HDI container resource definition to mta.yaml
- Configures the production CDS profile to use hana-cloud as the db kind

After running this command, your mta.yaml will define three components:

1. incident-management-srv (Node.js module — the CAP OData service)
- Deployed as a CF application
- Provides: srv-api (the service URL consumed by the Fiori app later)
- Requires: incident-management-db (the HDI container)

2. incident-management-db-deployer (hdb module — the schema deployer)
- A one-time deployer app that pushes the CDS schema to HANA
- Runs during deployment then stops (Stopped state is normal)
- Requires: incident-management-db

3. incident-management-db (resource — the HDI container)
- Type: com.sap.xs.hdi-container
- Service: hana, Plan: hdi-shared
- This is the actual schema container created inside your HANA Cloud instance (SHC_DB) that was set up in Part 3 


STEP 3 — BUILD THE MTA ARCHIVE

Run the MBT build command to compile the project into a deployable archive:

mbt build

This command:
- Reads the mta.yaml configuration
- Runs `npm install` and `npx cds build --production` to compile the CDS model
- Packages all modules into a single .mtar archive file

The output archive is created at:

mta_archives/incident-management_1.0.0.mtar

 

STEP 4 — DEPLOY TO CLOUD FOUNDRY

Make sure you are logged in to CF and targeting the correct space:

cf login -a <api endpoint>
cf target -o <your-org> -s dev

Now deploy the MTA archive:

cf deploy mta_archives/incident-management_1.0.0.mtar

CF will:
1. Create the HDI container service instance (incident-management-db)
2. Deploy and run the db-deployer to push the schema to HANA
3. Start the CAP service application (incident-management-srv)

Once deployment completes, navigate to your CF space in BTP Cockpit:

Trial Home →   f030ff54trial   → trial   → dev → Applications

You will see two applications in the "dev" space:

 

STEP 5 — VERIFY THE HDI CONTAINER INSTANCE

Navigate to:

Space: dev → Services → Instances

You should see the HDI container service instance that was automatically created during deployment:

 This HDI container lives inside the SHC_DB HANA Cloud instance we created in Part 3. CAP automatically created it during the cf deploy step.

 

STEP 6 — EXPLORE THE HANA TABLES IN DB EXPLORER

Now let's verify the schema was deployed correctly by exploring the tables in SAP HANA Database Explorer.

Open HANA Cloud Central → click "Open" on the SHC_DB instance →
select "SAP HANA Database Explorer".

In Database Explorer, the left panel shows your SHC-DB instance connected as DBADMIN. To view the HDI container tables, click the "+" (Add Instance) icon.

 

Select "HDI Container" as the Instance Type, filter by your org (f030ff54trial) and space (dev).

Select "incident-management-db" and click OK.

 

The HDI container is now added to the left panel. Expand it to see the Tables folder. You will find all the CDS entities have been deployed as HANA tables.

Click on SAP_CAPIRE_INCIDENTS_INCIDENTS to inspect its structure:


STEP 7 — RUNNING IN HYBRID MODE

Now that the CAP app is deployed and the HDI container exists in BTP, you can run your local development server connected directly to the cloud HANA database. This is the "hybrid" mode — your app runs locally but reads and writes real HANA Cloud data.

This is very useful for testing local code changes against production data before deploying again.

Step 1 — Bind your local project to the HDI container service instance:

cds bind -2 incident-management-db:key

What this does:
- Connects to Cloud Foundry and retrieves the service key for the "incident-management-db" HDI container instance
- Creates a service key on BTP (if one doesn't exist)
- Saves the HANA connection credentials (host, schema, user, password) into .cdsrc-private.json under the "hybrid" profile
- The .cdsrc-private.json file is local only — never commit it to git

Step 2 — Start the server in hybrid mode:

cds watch --profile hybrid

The terminal confirms the app is now connected to the real HANA Cloud database, showing:
- The HANA host and schema ID
- Driver: com.sap.db.jdbc.Driver (JDBC connection to HANA)
- Both ProcessorService and AdminService are being served

Your app on localhost:4004 now reads and writes directly to the HANA Cloud instance in BTP — the Fiori preview will show and save real data.


SUMMARY

In Part 4, we successfully:

✔ Configured package.json with three CDS profiles: development (SQLite), hybrid (local + HANA Cloud), production (CF + HANA)
✔ Ran cds add hana to wire the project for HANA Cloud and generate mta.yaml
✔ Built the deployable MTA archive using mbt build
✔ Deployed the CAP backend to Cloud Foundry using cf deploy
✔ Verified the two CF apps: incident-management-srv (Started) and incident-management-db-deployer (Stopped — expected)
✔ Confirmed the HDI container instance was created with 2 bindings
✔ Explored the HANA tables and seed data in SAP HANA Database Explorer
✔ Connected the local app to the HANA Cloud instance using hybrid mode

The CAP backend is now live on Cloud Foundry and backed by SAP HANA Cloud.
In Part 5 , we will build the Fiori Elements UI application and connect it to this deployed CAP service.

Destination name: destination-trial
