entry.title: Fullstack CAP Application with HANA Cloud (Decoupled Architecture) [Part-5]
entry.content:
Configuring the Destination in BTP

In Part 4 , we deployed the CAP backend to Cloud Foundry. It is now live and accessible via a public CF route URL.

In this Part, we will configure a BTP Destination — a named connection entry that acts as a pointer from BTP services to the deployed CAP backend URL.

This destination is the critical link between the Fiori Elements app (which we will deploy to the HTML5 Application Repository in Part 6) and the CAP OData service running on Cloud Foundry.


WHY IS A DESTINATION NEEDED?

In a decoupled architecture, the Fiori app and the CAP backend are deployed independently:

Fiori App (HTML5 Repo) ──► xs-app.json routes ──► Destination ──► CAP Service (CF)

When the browser loads the Fiori app and makes OData calls (e.g., GET /odata/v4/incidents-processor/Incidents), those requests are routed through the AppRouter via xs-app.json. The routing rule in xs-app.json says:

Any request matching ^/odata/(.*) → forward to "destination-trial"

The destination named "destination-trial" then resolves to the actual HTTPS URL of the CAP service on Cloud Foundry. This way, the Fiori app never needs to hardcode the backend URL — it just uses the destination name.

 

STEP 1 — NAVIGATE TO DESTINATIONS IN BTP COCKPIT

In the SAP BTP Cockpit, navigate to your Subaccount and go to:

Connectivity → Destinations

The Destinations page will open showing an empty list (All: 0) since no destinations have been created yet.

The left panel shows the context level:
trial - Destinations → trial (Read and Write access)

 

STEP 2 — CREATE A NEW DESTINATION

Click the "Create" button. A small dialog appears with three options:

From Scratch → Create a new destination manually by filling in the form From File → Import a destination from a previously exported config file Service Instance → Auto-create a destination from a BTP service instance

Select "From Scratch" since we will fill in the details manually.

 

STEP 3 — FIND THE CAP SERVICE URL

Before filling in the destination form, you need the URL of the deployed CAP service. Navigate to:

Space: dev → Applications → incident-management-srv → Application Overview

In the "Mapped Routes" section on the right, you will see the public CF route assigned to the CAP service.

  Copy this route URL — you will paste it as the destination URL in the next step.

STEP 4 — FILL IN THE DESTINATION DETAILS

Back on the Destinations page, fill in the form.

 

 

 WHY NoAuthentication?
In this tutorial setup with a trial account, we are using "dummy" auth in the CAP service (as configured in package.json).

For a productive setup, you would use OAuth2ClientCredentials or OAuth2UserTokenExchange with an XSUAA service instance to secure the backend properly.

Click "Save" to create the destination.

The destination is now listed in the Destinations page:

Name: destination-trial | Type: HTTP

HOW THE DESTINATION IS USED IN THE FIORI APP

The Fiori app references this destination by name in two key files:

xs-app.json (AppRouter routing rules):
- Any request to /odata/* is forwarded to "destination-trial"
- This routes all OData calls from the Fiori UI to the CAP service
- Authentication is handled via XSUAA

manifest.json (OData data source):
- The mainService data source points to /odata/v4/incidents-processor/
- This path matches the /odata/* routing rule in xs-app.json, so it will automatically be forwarded to the destination-trial destination and reach the CAP ProcessorService on Cloud Foundry

> In short: Fiori app calls /odata/v4/incidents-processor/Incidents
> → xs-app.json routes it to destination-trial
> → destination-trial resolves to the CF route of incident-management-srv
> → CAP service responds with HANA Cloud data


SUMMARY

In Part 5, we successfully:

✔ Navigated to the Destinations section in the BTP Subaccount
✔ Created a new HTTP destination named "destination-trial" from scratch
✔ Used the CF mapped route of incident-management-srv as the destination URL
✔ Understood how xs-app.json and manifest.json in the Fiori app reference this destination to route OData calls to the CAP backend

The destination is now the live bridge between the Fiori frontend and the CAP backend. In Part 6 , we will deploy the Fiori Elements app to the HTML5 Application Repository and access the complete end-to-end application.

entry.title: UI Composition with Application Frontend Service
entry.content:
As UI application developers, we often find ourselves implementing the same functionality across multiple applications. The natural instinct is to extract that common code into reusable files that can be shared between projects. Traditionally, this is done in one of the following ways:

  • Development time. Copy-pasting shared files directly into each application's source code. This is the easiest way to start, but a maintenance nightmare. Any change to the common logic requires patching and redeploying every application that uses it. On top of that, the duplicated files increase the size of each application and slow down deployments.
  • Build/deploy time. Publishing shared code as an NPM package. This solves the problem of maintaining changes in multiple places, but still requires rebuilding and redeploying all affected applications. It also complicates the release lifecycle, since packages and applications must be released in a specific order.
  • Runtime. Hosting the shared code separately and accessing it via URL:
    • Directly from the client—eliminates code duplication and avoids rebuilding or redeploying applications, but introduces complexity around CORS/CSP restrictions and authentication/session management.
    • Via a server-side proxy—keeps the same user session and avoids CORS/CSP issues, but adds an extra network hop for every request to the shared resources.

All of these approaches work with Application Frontend service. However, in this post I want to show you a more efficient way to achieve UI composition—one that is unique to UIs hosted on Application Frontend service. In short, it is a form of runtime server-side composition, but without the overhead of extra network hops.

To demonstrate the possibilities of application-to-application reuse, we will walk through three common use cases that call for UI composition.

Reusable Application / Component

This use case applies when you have control over the consuming application's source code and want to embed a piece of reusable logic into it. The goal is to benefit from automatic updates to the shared code while preserving the consuming application's URL as the entry point for end users.

Figure 1. Reusable Application

To set this up, the consuming application's xs-app.json needs a route that points to the reusable application. This route uses an "application" property that references another Application Frontend application by name, optionally followed by @ and a specific version. The "source" property contains either a specific resource path or a regular expression that is different from the catch-all (.*) pattern. Path rewriting via the "target" property is also supported. For this use case, the route pointing to the reusable application is placed before the routes pointing to static resources of the consuming application itself.

Here is an example of the consuming application's xs-app.json:

{
  "errorPage": [
    { "status": [404], "path": "/error/404.html" }
  ],
  "routes": [{
    "source": "^/error/(.*)",
    "target": "/common/$1",
    "application": "mylib@1.0.0"
  }, {
    "source": "^(/|/index.html)$",
    "target": "/index.html",
    "service": "app-front"
  }, {
    "source": "/assets/.*",
    "service": "app-front"
  }]
}

This configuration assumes that another Application Frontend application exists with "sap.app/id" set to "mylib" in its manifest.json, deployed in the same BTP subaccount. There is nothing special required in the xs-app.json or manifest.json of the reusable application. For example, if mylib has the following routes:

{
  "routes": [{
    "source": "^/common/(.*)",
    "target": "/dist/$1",
    "service": "app-front"
  }]
}

then a browser request for a resource that does not match any route "source" pattern in the xs-app.json of consuming application (app1) will be redirected to:

https:​//app1-xyzab.eu10.appfront.cloud.sap/error/404.html

and will serve the /dist/404.html file from the mylib application. Any follow-up requests from the error page (for example, to load an illustration image) will also be served from mylib, as long as they use relative paths. This way, you can reuse the same error pages across multiple Application Frontend applications.

Application Extension

This use case applies when you don't have control over—or are not allowed to change—the source code of an existing application, yet you need to create a very similar application with minor modifications. End users will access both the original and the extended application via separate URLs.

Figure 2. Application Extension

The implementation is very similar to the reusable application approach, but inverted: most requests to the extension application serve content from the original application, while the extension itself contains only the delta. In the extension's xs-app.json, the catch-all route points to the original application, and routes for specific paths that need to be overridden are placed before it.

The extension application's xs-app.json might look like this:

{
  "routes": [{
    "source": "^/view/App.view.xml",
    "service": "app-front"
  }, {
    "source": ".*",
    "application": "original"
  }]
}

In this example, the only static resource of extension application (besides xs-app.json and manifest.json) is a modified /view/App.view.xml. This lets you add, remove, or modify parts of the view while inheriting everything else from the original application.

UI Mashup

This use case is about integrating multiple existing UIs and data sources into a single unified application. The mashup has its own URL and behaves as a standalone application from a lifecycle perspective, yet it contains no UI artifacts of its own—only xs-app.json and manifest.json.

This may sound complex at first, but it is essentially a combination of the previous two patterns: the mashup application extends a base application, but instead of hosting override resources itself, it delegates to other applications that act as reusable components.

Figure 3. UI Mashup

Let's look at a concrete example. Imagine a preview application that includes several embedded apps (deployed as part of the preview application itself) and a static apps.json file listing them. The preview application displays whichever embedded app the user selects inside a mobile shell, simulating how the app would look on a real mobile device. Now suppose you want this preview to be able to show any Application Frontend application deployed to your BTP subaccount, with the list of available applications served dynamically from a backend configured in the apps destination. A mashup application solves this.

Consider the following xs-app.json for the mashup application:

{
  "routes": [{
    "source": "^/apps.json",
    "destination": "apps"
  }, {
    "source": "^/app/(.*)",
    "application": "$1"
  }, {
    "source": ".*",
    "application": "preview"
  }]
}

With this configuration, the "application" property in the second route is resolved dynamically based on the request path. The static /apps.json is replaced with dynamic content from the backend, while all other requests fall through to the preview application.

Visibility

The application-to-application reuse relationships are part of Application Frontend application metadata, accessible via the API, CLI, and BTP Cockpit UI (on the application version dependencies screen). Application Frontend service provides not only design-time information about which application depends on which, but also live availability status of all dependencies. This makes it easy to spot issues—such as a missing reusable application or a stopped base application—without digging into the source code or analyzing runtime logs.

Figure 4. BTP Cockpit Application Frontend Dependencies View

Conclusion

The application-to-application reuse feature of Application Frontend service is a powerful mechanism for UI composition that reduces both development and operational costs by improving:

  • Lifecycle management—There is no required order for releasing reusable and consuming applications. Consuming applications do not need to be redeployed to pick up new versions of shared code.
  • Security—No complex CORS/CSP configuration is needed. The browser treats reusable resources as if they were an integral part of the consuming application. A shared user session between consuming and reusable applications ensures consistent sign-out without orphaned "zombie" sessions.
  • Performance—Since all participants in the composition are Application Frontend applications, there are no redundant network calls from the runtime to itself. Application Frontend is aware of all deployed applications and can perform recursive routing target resolution without making extra outbound requests.
  • Extensibility—Base applications do not need to define extensibility points, hooks, or any other upfront preparations. You don't have to touch existing applications. Every Application Frontend application can be reused, extended, or composed into a mashup out of the box.

entry.title: Moving HTML5 Applications to Application Frontend Service
entry.content:
This blog walks you through the changes you need to make when transitioning an MTA-based HTML5 application from the hosting services of HTML5 Repository and the managed approuter to the new Application Frontend service, and explains why the transition is worthwhile.

A Quick Recap: What Is Application Frontend?

Application Frontend is a SaaS application on SAP BTP for hosting, serving, and operating frontend applications. It was introduced as part of the SAP Build release and is designed to be a single point of entry for UI application management — bringing back the simplicity from the Neo HTML5 Runtime to the multi-cloud environment.

Check out this introduction blog for more details Introducing Application Frontend Service .

Key benefits of using Application Frontend

  • Versioning: Neo-style multi-version support with multiple active versions and a configurable default. You can test a new version in production without disrupting existing users.
  • Faster deployments: Deployments complete in seconds via CLI or API, ideal for fast dev test cycles.
  • Full application lifecycle control: Manage, monitor, and operate applications from the BTP Cockpit, CLI, or API — with observability and fine-grained control per application.
  • Simpler MTA setup: The destination-content module and all its service key scaffolding disappear — fewer modules, fewer service keys, and less configuration to maintain.
  • Visibility into used services: A “binding-like” behavior provides a clear view from the cockpit or CLI into the dependencies of your application.
  • And many other features that make your development experience easier.

Should you fancy using Application Frontend and like to move an existing application already deployed to the HTML5 Repository to Application Frontend, here are the steps to do it.

What Changes Are Needed?

Moving your application from HTML5 Repo to Application Frontend requires some changes in the application deployment and routing descriptors – the mta.yaml and xs-app.json.

The main change is in the mta.yaml which becomes much simpler - Application Frontend eliminates the need for instance-level destinations for storing credentials.

With HTML5 Repo, credentials for required services such as XSUAA, Workflow, and other services had to be exposed as destinations so the managed approuter could reach them. This required a dedicated module that created service keys and mapped them to instance-level destinations (module myApp-destination-content in the example below).

With Application Frontend, service credentials are stored directly within the application. You bind your services (XSUAA, Workflow, etc.) directly to the app-content module, and Application Frontend takes care of the rest.

The result: fewer modules, fewer service keys, and less configuration to maintain.

Note: the following example refers to an older work mode used with HTML5 repository service. If you already use the newer methodology where credentials destination is not used anymore, you can skip steps 1 and 2.

Your Current MTA Descriptor (html5-apps-repo)

Let's look at a sample MTA descriptor for deploying an HTML5 application. The application uses a destination to a backend service, an XSUAA instance, and the Workflow service.

_schema-version: "3.2"
ID: myApp
version: 0.0.1

modules:
  # Module that creates instance-level destinations with credentials
  - name: myApp-destination-content
    type: com.sap.application.content
    requires:
      - name: myApp-destination
        parameters:
          content-target: true
      - name: myApp-html-repo-host
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: myApp-html-repo-host-key
      - name: myApp-xsuaa
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: myApp-xsuaa-key
      - name: myApp-workflow-service
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: myApp-workflow-key
    parameters:
      content:
        instance:
          destinations:
            # Destination with app-host credentials
            - Name: myApp-html-repo-host-destination
              ServiceInstanceName: myApp-html5-app-host-service
              ServiceKeyName: myApp-html-repo-host-key
              sap.cloud.service: business.solution.service
              Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange
            # Destination with XSUAA credentials
            - Name: myApp-xsuaa-destination
              ServiceInstanceName: myApp-xsuaa-service
              ServiceKeyName: myApp-xsuaa-key
              sap.cloud.service: business.solution.service
            # Destination pointing to Workflow reuse service instance
            - Name: myApp-workflow-destination
              Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange
              ServiceInstanceName: myApp-workflow-service
              ServiceKeyName: myApp-workflow-key
          existing_destinations_policy: ignore
    build-parameters:
      no-source: true

  # Module that deploys HTML5 application content
  - name: myApp-app-content
    type: com.sap.application.content
    path: .
    requires:
      - name: myApp-html5-repo-host
        parameters:
          content-target: true
    build-parameters:
      build-result: resources
      requires:
        - artifacts:
            - html5-app.zip
          name: html5-app
          target-path: resources/

  # HTML5 application module
  - name: html5-app
    type: html5
    path: html5-app
    build-parameters:
      build-result: dist
      builder: custom
      commands:
        - npm install
        - npm run build:cf
      supported-platforms: []

resources:
  # Destination service instance 
  - name: myApp-destination
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      config:
        HTML5Runtime_enabled: true
        init_data:
          instance:
            destinations:
              # Destination to the backend service
              - Authentication: NoAuthentication
                Name: backend-api
                ProxyType: Internet
                Type: HTTP
                URL: https://backend-api.example.com
            existing_destinations_policy: update
        version: 1.0.0
      service: destination
      service-plan: lite

  # HTML5 Repo app-host service instance
  - name: myApp-html5-repo-host
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-host

  # XSUAA service instance
  - name: myApp-xsuaa
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      path: ./xs-security.json
      service: xsuaa
      service-plan: application

  # Workflow reuse service instance
  - name: myApp-workflow-service
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: workflow
      service-plan: lite

parameters:
  deploy_mode: html5-repo

Here are the needed Steps

1. Delete the Entire `myApp-destination-content` Module

With app-front, credentials for dependent services are stored directly with the application, so this destination is no longer needed.

Action: Remove the myApp-destination-content module completely.

2. Update the `myApp-app-content` Module

The app-content module now needs to:

  • Bind directly to the destination, XSUAA, and Workflow service instances (no longer via destinations)
  • Reference the app-front service instead of html-repo-host as the content target
  • Keep everything else unchanged (build parameters, artifact dependencies)

Current `myApp-app-content`:

requires:
  - name: myApp-html-repo-host
    parameters:
      content-target: true

Update to:

requires:
  - name: myApp-xsuaa
  - name: myApp-workflow
  - name: myApp-destination-service  
  - name: myApp-app-front
    parameters:
      content-target: true

3. Replace the `html5-repo-host` Resource

The HTML5 repository service (html5-apps-repo) is replaced with the Application Frontend service (app-front).

Current resource:

- name: myApp-html5-repo-host
  type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
  parameters:
    service: html5-apps-repo
    service-plan: app-host

Replace with:

- name: myApp-app-front
  type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
  parameters:
    service: app-front
    service-plan: developer

4. Remove `HTML5Runtime_enabled` from Destination Service

The destination service is still needed to point to the backend, but the HTML5Runtime_enabled: true flag is no longer required.

Changed destination config:

config:
#  HTML5Runtime_enabled: true   ** This line is not needed anymore **
  init_data:
    instance:
      destinations:
        - Authentication: NoAuthentication
          Name: backend-api
          ProxyType: Internet
          Type: HTTP
          URL: https://backend-api.example.com
        existing_destinations_policy: update
  version: 1.0.0

5. Update xs-app.json

The xs-app.json file inside your HTML5 application controls how routes are handled. Routes that serve static content reference the hosting service by name — this needs to change from html5-apps-repo-rt to app-front.

Before:

{
  "source": "^/index.html$",
  "target": "/index.html",
  "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
},
{
  "source": "^(.*)$",
  "target": "$1",
  "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt"
}

Update to:

{
  "source": "^/index.html$",
  "target": "/index.html",
  "service": "app-front",
},
{
  "source": "^(.*)$",
  "target": "$1",
  "service": "app-front"
}

Action: Replace every instance of "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt" with "service": "app-front". Routes pointing to backend destinations are unaffected.

That it!! No other changes are needed.

What Stays the Same

The following require no changes:

  • The HTML5 application module itself (html5-app) build commands, paths, etc.
  • XSUAA service instance configuration
  • Workflow service instance configuration
  • Backend destinations that do not carry a sap.cloud.service attribute

To Sum Up

Moving an existing UI application from HTML5 Repo to AppFront is a simple, straightforward process that will not impact the business logic of your application.

Note that the URL of the application will change, so bookmarks will have to be updated. If your application is integrated into an SAP Build Work Zone site, these settings will have to be updated as well.

The New MTA Descriptor (app-front)

For reference, here is the full descriptor after applying all required changes.

_schema-version: "3.2"
ID: myApp-id
version: 0.0.1

modules:
  # Module that deploys HTML5 application content
  - name: myApp-app-content
    type: com.sap.application.content
    path: .
    requires:
      - name: myApp-xsuaa
      - name: myApp-workflow
      - name: myApp-app-front
        parameters:
          content-target: true
    build-parameters:
      build-result: resources
      requires:
        - artifacts:
            - html5-app.zip
          name: html5-app
          target-path: resources/

  # HTML5 application module
  - name: html5-app
    type: html5
    path: html5-app
    build-parameters:
      build-result: dist
      builder: custom
      commands:
        - npm install
        - npm run build:cf
      supported-platforms: []

resources:
  - name: myApp-backend-destination
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      config:
        init_data:
          instance:
            destinations:
              # Backend destination without sap.cloud.service
              - Authentication: NoAuthentication
                Name: backend-api
                ProxyType: Internet
                Type: HTTP
                URL: https://backend-api.example.com
            existing_destinations_policy: update
        version: 1.0.0
      service: destination
      service-plan: lite

  # HTML5 app-front service instance
  - name: myApp-app-front
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: app-front
      service-plan: developer

  # XSUAA service instance
  - name: myApp-xsuaa
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      path: ./xs-security.json
      service: xsuaa
      service-plan: application

  # Workflow reuse service instance
  - name: myApp-workflow-service
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: workflow
      service-plan: lite

entry.title: From Code to Strategy: How MCP, CPI, and Lightweight Agents Unlock AI‑Driven SAP Integrations
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Cloud Platform Integration (CPI) allows enterprises to connect diverse systems through iFlows — integration flows that define how data moves and transforms between endpoints. By combining CPI with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and a lightweight Agent, we can expose SAP processes as consumable services — enabling seamless orchestration, automation, and intelligent interaction across enterprise systems.

 

Understanding the Components

SAP Cloud Platform Integration (CPI)

SAP CPI is the integration backbone of the SAP ecosystem. It enables secure, scalable, and real-time data exchange between SAP and non-SAP systems. In this architecture, CPI acts as the execution layer, where business logic resides. The iFlow processes requests coming from the MCP Server, performs necessary transformations, and interacts with SAP backend systems such as S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, or Finance modules.

In the AI world: CPI provides the structured data foundation that intelligent agents rely on. By exposing iFlows as APIs, it allows AI systems to access enterprise data securely and contextually — bridging traditional ERP with modern AI-driven automation.

 

Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server

The MCP Server is the middleware bridge between the Agent and SAP CPI. It defines “tools” — essentially API endpoints — that the Agent can call to trigger specific SAP processes. It handles authentication, routing, and error management, ensuring that requests from the Agent are properly formatted and securely transmitted to CPI.

In the AI world: MCP acts as the contextual translator between natural language and enterprise APIs. It enables AI agents to understand what business functions are available and how to invoke them, making enterprise systems conversational and intelligent.

 

Copilot Agent

The Agent is the frontline interface — a lightweight application (built with FastAPI or similar frameworks) that interacts with users or other systems. It consumes the MCP tools and provides a simple way to trigger SAP processes, either through a web UI or API calls.

In the AI world: The Agent represents the intelligence layer — capable of interpreting user intent, orchestrating workflows, and connecting to enterprise data through MCP and CPI. It’s the component that transforms static APIs into dynamic, AI-driven interactions.

 

Key Steps

1. Expose the iFlow in SAP CPI

  • Design and deploy your iFlow (e.g., invoice retrieval or employee data).

  • Ensure it’s accessible via HTTPS with proper authentication.

2. Create the MCP Server

  • Define tools mapping to CPI endpoints.

  • Configure the MCP server to expose these tools securely.

  • Example endpoint: http://localhost:8000/tools/sayHello

3. Consume with an Agent

  • Build a lightweight Agent using FastAPI.

  • Connect it to the MCP server and expose an endpoint like http://localhost:9000/agent/sayHello.

  • Provide a simple UI for users to trigger CPI processes.

 

Tools Used

  • SAP CPI → iFlow design and deployment

  • MCP Server → Tool definition and orchestration

  • FastAPI → Agent development

  • OAuth2 / SAP IAS → Authentication and security

 

Architecture Overview

Embed your architecture diagram here showing the flow: User → Copilot Agent → MCP Server → SAP CPI → SAP Backend Systems

Figure 1: End-to-end architecture connecting the Agent, MCP Server, and SAP CPI iFlow.

Step: Create a Simple iFlow in SAP CPI

Design a basic iFlow in SAP Cloud Platform Integration (CPI) that accepts a name as input payload and returns a greeting message. For example, if the payload contains "Dibyajyoti", the iFlow should respond with "Hello Dibyajyoti".

Once the development is complete, deploy the iFlow to generate the endpoint URL. This URL will be used later by the MCP Server and Copilot Agent to invoke the iFlow and integrate it into the overall architecture.

"https://<SUBACCOUNT>.it-cpitrial06-rt.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/http/hello"

Step 2: Test the iFlow Endpoint in Postman

Once the iFlow is deployed in SAP CPI, you’ll receive an endpoint URL. To validate it, use Postman:

  1. Open Postman and create a new request.

  2. Set the method to POST (or GET, depending on your iFlow design).

  3. Enter the endpoint URL generated during deployment (e.g., https://cpi.example.com/http/endpoint/sayHello).

  4. Authentication:

    • Username → Client ID

    • Password → Client Secret These credentials are provided when you configure the CPI tenant and are required for secure access.

  5. Payload:

    • In the request body, pass the input JSON or text payload (e.g., { "name": "Dibyajyoti" }).

  6. Send the request and verify the response.

    • Expected output: Hello Dibyajyoti

 

Step 3: Set Up the MCP Environment

Before working with the MCP Server, ensure your development environment is ready. You’ll need the following installed on your system:

  • Python (version 3.9 or above recommended)

  • PIP (Python package manager)

  • Visual Studio Code (for editing and running your project)


Step 4: Create the Project Folder Structure

To organize your MCP setup, create the following folders:

  1. Main Project Folder

    • Name: MCPPROJECT

  2. Subfolders inside MCPPROJECT

    • SAP_MCP_SERVER → Contains the MCP Server files (server.py, .env, requirements.txt)

    • COPILOT_AGENT → Contains the Agent files (agent.py, templates/index.html, requirements.txt)

 

SAP_MCP_SERVER

.env---->

requirements.txt---->

server.py---->

COPILOT_AGENT

requirements.txt------>

agent.py------->

create a subfolder

index.html--------->

 

Step 5: Run the MCP Server and Copilot Agent

Inside sap_mcp_server

Install dependencies and start the MCP Server:

pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn server:app --reload --port 8000

 

  • pip install -r requirements.txt → Installs all required Python packages.

  • uvicorn server:app --reload --port 8000 → Launches the MCP Server on port 8000 with auto-reload enabled.

Inside copilot_agent

Install dependencies and start the Copilot Agent:

pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn agent:app --reload --port 9000
​

 

  • pip install -r requirements.txt → Installs Agent dependencies.

  • uvicorn agent:app --reload --port 9000 → Launches the Agent on port 9000 with auto-reload enabled.

Test the Agent

Once both services are running, open the Agent URL in your browser:

http://localhost:9000/

 This will load the Agent’s web interface, allowing you to trigger the MCP tools and ultimately invoke the SAP CPI iFlow.

 

Conclusion

By exposing SAP CPI iFlows through an MCP Server and consuming them with an Agent, enterprises can create a modular, API-driven integration layer. This approach simplifies access to SAP processes, improves reusability, and lays the foundation for AI-powered enterprise automation — where intelligent agents can interact with SAP systems naturally, securely, and efficiently.

Regards,

Dibyajyoti Nanda

entry.title: SAP UI5 AND FIORI VERSION MANAGER
entry.content:
SAPUI5 Version Management Made Easy with UI5 Lifecycle

If you work with multiple SAPUI5 applications in a single monorepo, you've probably run into situations where version management becomes tedious.

Perhaps you need to:

  • Increase the application version of several SAPUI5 applications before deployment
  • Upgrade SAPUI5 runtime versions across multiple applications
  • Update the version used by SAP Build Work Zone
  • Keep your bootstrap URL aligned with the configured SAPUI5 runtime
  • Manage several applications within the same repository

While none of these tasks are difficult individually, they quickly become repetitive and error-prone when performed across multiple applications.

To help simplify these activities, I created UI5 Lifecycle, an open-source npm package that automates common SAPUI5 version management tasks.

The project is available on npm: 👉ui5-lifecycle - npm  

How It Works

UI5 Lifecycle focuses on two main areas:

1. Application Version Management

The package can automatically detect changed SAPUI5 applications using Git and update the application version stored in:

 
{
  "sap.app": {
    "applicationVersion": {
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
  }
}

Version bumps can be performed as:

  • Patch
  • Minor
  • Major

using semantic versioning principles.

 

2. SAPUI5 Runtime Management

The package can also manage SAPUI5 runtime versions.

Rather than relying on hardcoded values, UI5 Lifecycle retrieves the latest available SAPUI5 and LTS versions from SAP's published version metadata here maintainace status overview

This makes it easy to keep applications aligned with SAP's currently available releases.

  2.1 SAP Build Work Zone Runtime Version Management

Many SAP developers are unaware that applications running in SAP Build Work Zone can specify the SAPUI5 runtime through the following entry in manifest.json:

{...,
  "sap.platform.cf": {
    "ui5VersionNumber": "1.150.0"
  }
}

This property determines which SAPUI5 runtime version is loaded by Build Work Zone.

UI5 Lifecycle can automatically maintain this value and upgrade it either to:

  • The latest SAPUI5 version
  • The latest SAPUI5 Long-Term Support (LTS) version

   2.2 Bootstrap Synchronization

UI5 Lifecycle also updates the SAPUI5 bootstrap URL inside index.html. when either the latest or lts version is demanded.

Before:

<script
  id="sap-ui-bootstrap"
  src="https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com/1.149.1/resources/sap-ui-core.js">

After:

<script
  id="sap-ui-bootstrap"
  src="https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com/1.150.0/resources/sap-ui-core.js">
</script>

This helps ensure that the bootstrap URL remains aligned with the runtime version configured in manifest.json.

Installation

npm install -g ui5-lifecycle

Verify the installation:

ui5-lifecycle latest-ui5
 

Available Commands

1. Get the Latest SAPUI5 Version

ui5-lifecycle latest-ui5

Example:

1.150.0

2. Get the Latest SAPUI5 LTS Version

ui5-lifecycle lts-ui5

Example:

1.148.5

 

Interactive Application Release

ui5-lifecycle release

Example: CustomerApp currently Deployed on the BTP has version (1.0.1) and needs a version bump, using the ui5-lifecycle, the versions could be bumped in this manner

customerApp(1.0.0)
p  patch  1.0.1 -> 1.0.2
m  minor  1.0.1 -> 1.1.0
M  major  1.0.1 -> 2.0.0
s  skip

Select bump type [p/m/M/s]:
 

Upgrade to the Latest SAPUI5 Runtime

ui5-lifecycle upgrade-ui5-latest --all

This updates:

{
  "sap.platform.cf": {
    "ui5VersionNumber": "1.150.0"
  }
}

 AT the time of making this post 1.150.0 is the latest SAP UI5 version which would change in the future. But the tool always fetches the latest one as released by SAP at Available SAPUI5 versions on SAP Business Technology Platform

 

Upgrade to Latest SAPUI5 LTS Runtime

ui5-lifecycle upgrade-ui5-lts --all

This updates:

{
  "sap.platform.cf": {
    "ui5VersionNumber": "1.148.5"
  }
}

 where 1.148.5 is the latest LTS ui5 version.

 

Dry Run Application Release

Dry run is used to preview how the tool works without making any updates in your application. Example

 

ui5-lifecycle release --dry-run

shows:

customerApp: 1.0.0 -> 1.0.1 (patch)

Dry run only. No files were changed.

Dry Run SAPUI5 Runtime Upgrade

ui5-lifecycle upgrade-ui5-latest --all-dry-run

Shows:

Using the UI5 version: 1.150.0

UI5 Upgrade summary: 

customerApp:
1.149.1 -> 1.150.0

Dry run only. No files were changed.

 

Supported Project Structure

The supported project structure for this tool is shown below:

app/
├── CustomerApp/
│   └── webapp/
│       ├── manifest.json
│       └── index.html

├── OrderApp/
│   └── webapp/
│       ├── manifest.json
│       └── index.html

Conclusion

UI5 Lifecycle was created to simplify common SAPUI5 maintenance activities across multiple applications.

It currently provides:

✅Application version management

✅SAPUI5 runtime upgrades

✅SAP Build Work Zone runtime management

✅Bootstrap synchronization

✅Git-based application detection

✅Dry-run support

I welcome feedback, suggestions, and contributions from the SAPUI5 community.

👉GitHub Issues: Create an Issue

entry.title: How I Enabled Support of bot Standalone and Managed Approuters in One SAPUI5 and SAP CAP Application
entry.content:
Supporting Standalone and Managed Approuters in One SAPUI5 and SAP CAP Application

Introduction

While developing an SAPUI5 application on SAP BTP, I encountered a requirement that initially appeared straightforward:

  • The application should be directly accessible through a standalone approuter.
  • The same application should also be available through SAP Build Work Zone using its managed approuter.
  • Both entry points should use the same SAPUI5 codebase and SAP CAP backend.
  • Authentication, authorization, and OData communication should work consistently in both environments.

The application worked correctly when accessed through the standalone approuter. However, when I opened the same application from SAP Build Work Zone, I started encountering HTTP 404 errors, authentication failures, incorrect OData paths, and Content Security Policy issues with SAPUI5 VizFrame charts.

I initially assumed that because both runtime models use an xs-app.json file, the same routing configuration and absolute OData URLs would work in both environments. I eventually discovered that this assumption was incorrect.

The standalone and managed approuters serve the application from different URL contexts. This seemingly small difference directly affects how frontend service URLs are resolved.

In this article, I explain the architecture I designed and developed to support both approuter models using:

  • A single SAPUI5 codebase
  • A single SAP CAP service
  • XSUAA-based authentication
  • User-token propagation
  • SAP Destination service
  • HTML5 Application Repository
  • SAP Build Work Zone
  • Separate routing configurations
  • Runtime-aware OData URL resolution

This article is based on a real implementation and includes the design decisions, dead ends, configuration, code, and troubleshooting lessons from that experience.

The problem I was trying to solve

The application needed to support two access patterns.

Direct application access

Users should be able to open the application through a dedicated Cloud Foundry route exposed by a standalone approuter.

The request flow should be:

Browser
   |
   v
Standalone Approuter
   |
   +---- Serves the SAPUI5 application
   |
   +---- Forwards OData requests
   |
   v
SAP CAP Service

SAP Build Work Zone access

The same application should be available as an SAP Fiori application inside SAP Build Work Zone.

The request flow should be:

Browser
   |
   v
SAP Build Work Zone
   |
   v
Managed Approuter
   |
   +---- Loads the application from the HTML5 Application Repository
   |
   +---- Resolves the backend destination
   |
   v
SAP CAP Service

I wanted to avoid maintaining separate SAPUI5 applications or separate frontend builds for these two environments.

The first issue I encountered

My application initially used root-relative OData paths:

const SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/my-service/";

This worked correctly through the standalone approuter because the application and the OData route were available from the same host root.

For example:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/odata/v4/my-service/

However, the managed approuter uses an application-specific prefix when serving an application from the HTML5 Application Repository.

A simplified managed-approuter URL can look like this:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/index.html

The corresponding OData request may need to retain that prefix:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

When I used a leading slash:

/odata/v4/my-service/

the browser resolved the request from the host root and discarded the application prefix.

The request therefore became:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/odata/v4/my-service/

instead of:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

This resulted in an HTTP 404 response.

The most surprising part of the investigation was that a single leading slash determined whether the application worked or failed. Because the same URL worked through the standalone approuter, I initially investigated destination configuration and XSUAA authorization instead of URL resolution.

The design decision

I considered using environment-specific service URLs:

if (managedApprouter) {
    // Use managed-approuter URL
} else {
    // Use standalone-approuter URL
}

Another option was to maintain separate frontend builds for each runtime.

I decided against both approaches because they would:

  • Duplicate configuration
  • Introduce environment-specific code
  • Make deployments harder to maintain
  • Increase the risk of one version behaving differently from the other
  • Require changes whenever an application name or route changed

Instead, I designed a URL resolver that derives the service URL from the SAPUI5 component’s actual runtime location.

This allows the application to preserve the managed-approuter prefix while still supporting local CAP execution and the standalone approuter.

Project structure

The relevant project structure is:

project-root/
|
|-- app/
|   |
|   |-- my-ui5-app/
|       |
|       |-- webapp/
|       |   |-- controller/
|       |   |-- model/
|       |   |   |-- serviceUrl.js
|       |   |-- Component.js
|       |   |-- manifest.json
|       |   |-- index.html
|       |
|       |-- xs-app.json
|
|-- router/
|   |-- package.json
|   |-- xs-app.json
|
|-- srv/
|   |-- service.cds
|   |-- service.js
|
|-- xs-security.json
|-- mta.yaml
|-- package.json

Two xs-app.json files are intentionally maintained:

  • router/xs-app.json configures the standalone approuter.
  • app/my-ui5-app/xs-app.json configures the managed-approuter runtime.

Although the files have similar backend routes, they serve frontend content differently.

Standalone approuter implementation

Standalone approuter package

The standalone approuter is a Node.js Cloud Foundry application using @SAP/approuter.

The router/package.json can be defined as follows:

{
  "name": "my-standalone-approuter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "@sap/approuter": "^20.0.0"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js"
  }
}

The approuter itself does not contain application business logic. It handles responsibilities such as:

  • User authentication
  • Route matching
  • Forwarding requests
  • Token propagation
  • Serving frontend resources

Standalone xs-app.json

The standalone approuter serves the SAPUI5 application from its local webapp directory and forwards OData requests to the SAP CAP service.

{
  "welcomeFile": "index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/api-docs(.*)$",
      "target": "/api-docs$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "localDir": "webapp",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
    }
  ]
}

OData route

The following route captures requests beginning with /odata/:

{
  "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
  "target": "/odata/$1",
  "destination": "srv-api",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "csrfProtection": false
}

For example:

/odata/v4/my-service/Requests

is forwarded to:

<srv-api>/odata/v4/my-service/Requests

Frontend route

The final route serves the SAPUI5 files:

{
  "source": "^/(.*)$",
  "localDir": "webapp",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
}

This works because the standalone approuter module contains a copy of the built SAPUI5 webapp content.

Managed approuter implementation

In the managed-approuter scenario, I did not serve the frontend from the standalone router’s local directory.

Instead:

  1. The SAPUI5 application is built.
  2. The application is packaged as a ZIP archive.
  3. The archive is uploaded to the HTML5 Application Repository.
  4. SAP Build Work Zone discovers the application.
  5. The managed approuter loads it from the repository.
  6. Backend requests are forwarded through a destination.

Managed xs-app.json

The managed-approuter configuration belongs to the HTML5 application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/api-docs(.*)$",
      "target": "/api-docs$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^(.*)$",
      "target": "$1",
      "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
    }
  ]
}

The important difference is the frontend route:

{
  "source": "^(.*)$",
  "target": "$1",
  "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa"
}

Instead of using:

"localDir": "webapp"

the managed approuter loads the application through:

"service": "html5-apps-repo-rt"

This distinction is fundamental.

Runtime Frontend source
Standalone approuterLocal application directory
Managed approuterHTML5 Application Repository runtime

Dynamic OData URL resolution

The key part of my design was to stop treating the OData endpoint as a fixed root-relative URL.

Instead of this:

const SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/my-service/";

I used a relative service path:

const SERVICE_URL = "odata/v4/my-service/";

I then introduced a reusable SAPUI5 URL-resolution module.

serviceUrl.js

sap.ui.define([], () => {
    "use strict";

    const LOCAL_CAP_APP_PATH = /\/my-ui5-app(?:\/webapp)?\/?$/;

    function resolve(sUri) {
        const sRelativeUri = String(sUri || "").replace(/^\/+/, "");

        const oComponentBaseUrl = new URL(
            sap.ui.require.toUrl("my/ui5/app/"),
            window.location.href
        );

        /*
         * During local CAP execution, the UI may be served below:
         *
         * /my-ui5-app/webapp
         *
         * while the CAP OData service is exposed from:
         *
         * /odata
         */
        if (LOCAL_CAP_APP_PATH.test(oComponentBaseUrl.pathname)) {
            return new URL(
                `/${sRelativeUri}`,
                oComponentBaseUrl.origin
            ).toString();
        }

        /*
         * For a managed approuter, retain the HTML5 application
         * prefix by resolving the path relative to the component.
         */
        return new URL(
            sRelativeUri,
            oComponentBaseUrl
        ).toString();
    }

    return {
        resolve
    };
});

Replace the following values with your application-specific values:

/my-ui5-app/

and:

"my/ui5/app/"

The namespace should correspond to the SAPUI5 application namespace.

Why this resolver works

Local CAP runtime

Suppose the application is served locally from:

http://localhost:4004/my-ui5-app/webapp/

The resolver recognizes the local CAP application path and produces:

http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/my-service/

Standalone approuter

Suppose the application is served from:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/

The service URL resolves to:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/odata/v4/my-service/

Managed approuter

Suppose the SAPUI5 component is served from:

https://<managed-host>/<application-prefix>/

The relative service path resolves to:

https://<managed-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

The managed-approuter application prefix remains intact.

Using the resolver in the SAPUI5 application

The service constants should not start with /:

const SERVICE_V2_URL = "odata/v2/my-service/";
const SERVICE_V4_URL = "odata/v4/my-service/";

The resolver can then be imported into a controller or component.

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/UIComponent",
    "my/ui5/app/model/serviceUrl"
], function (
    UIComponent,
    serviceUrl
) {
    "use strict";

    return UIComponent.extend("my.ui5.app.Component", {
        metadata: {
            manifest: "json"
        },

        init: function () {
            UIComponent.prototype.init.apply(this, arguments);

            const sServiceUrl = serviceUrl.resolve(
                "odata/v4/my-service/"
            );

            console.log("Resolved service URL:", sServiceUrl);

            this.getRouter().initialize();
        }
    });
});

It can also be used for direct fetch calls:

const sUrl = serviceUrl.resolve(
    "odata/v4/my-service/getDashboardData"
);

fetch(sUrl, {
    method: "GET",
    credentials: "include",
    headers: {
        "Accept": "application/json"
    }
})
    .then(function (oResponse) {
        if (!oResponse.ok) {
            throw new Error(
                `Request failed with status ${oResponse.status}`
            );
        }

        return oResponse.json();
    })
    .then(function (oData) {
        console.log(oData);
    });

XSUAA authentication configuration

The application uses XSUAA for user authentication and role-based authorization.

A simplified xs-security.json can look like this:

{
  "xsappname": "my-application",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "name": "$XSAPPNAME.User",
      "description": "Application user access"
    },
    {
      "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin",
      "description": "Application administrator access"
    }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    {
      "name": "User",
      "description": "Application user",
      "scope-references": [
        "$XSAPPNAME.User"
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "Admin",
      "description": "Application administrator",
      "scope-references": [
        "$XSAPPNAME.User",
        "$XSAPPNAME.Admin"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

After deployment:

  1. Create the required role collections.
  2. Add the generated role templates.
  3. Assign the role collections to the relevant users or identity-provider groups.

A successful login only confirms that the identity provider authenticated the user. It does not automatically mean that the user has every application scope.

MTA configuration

The MTA contains the following major components:

SAP CAP service
Standalone approuter
SAPUI5 HTML5 module
HTML5 application content deployer
Destination content module
XSUAA service
Destination service
HTML5 repository host
HTML5 repository runtime

The following excerpts show the important relationships.

SAP CAP service module

modules:
  - name: my-application-srv
    type: nodejs
    path: gen/srv

    provides:
      - name: srv-api
        properties:
          srv-url: ${default-url}

    requires:
      - name: my-application-auth

    parameters:
      buildpack: nodejs_buildpack
      memory: 512M

The service exposes its runtime URL through the srv-api dependency:

provides:
  - name: srv-api
    properties:
      srv-url: ${default-url}

Standalone approuter module

  - name: my-application-router
    type: approuter.nodejs
    path: gen/router

    requires:
      - name: srv-api
        group: destinations
        properties:
          name: srv-api
          url: ~{srv-url}
          forwardAuthToken: true

      - name: my-application-auth

      - name: my-application-destination

      - name: my-application-html5-runtime

The following configuration propagates the logged-in user’s token to the CAP service:

forwardAuthToken: true

Without token forwarding, the CAP service may receive an anonymous or technically incomplete request and return HTTP 401 or 403.

SAPUI5 HTML5 module

  - name: my-ui5-app
    type: html5
    path: app/my-ui5-app

    build-parameters:
      builder: custom
      commands:
        - npm ci
        - npm run build
      supported-platforms: []
      build-result: dist

HTML5 application deployer

  - name: my-application-app-content
    type: com.sap.application.content
    path: .

    requires:
      - name: my-application-html5-host
        parameters:
          content-target: true

    build-parameters:
      build-result: resources
      requires:
        - name: my-ui5-app
          artifacts:
            - my-ui5-app.zip
          target-path: resources/

This module uploads the built SAPUI5 application to the HTML5 Application Repository.

Destination content module

  - name: my-application-destination-content
    type: com.sap.application.content

    requires:
      - name: my-application-destination
        parameters:
          content-target: true

      - name: my-application-html5-host
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: my-application-html5-host-key

      - name: my-application-auth
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: my-application-auth-key

      - name: srv-api

    parameters:
      content:
        instance:
          destinations:
            - Name: srv-api
              Type: HTTP
              ProxyType: Internet
              URL: ~{srv-api/srv-url}
              Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange
              HTML5.DynamicDestination: true
              HTML5.ForwardAuthToken: true

          existing_destinations_policy: update

For the managed-approuter flow, I used:

Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange

This allows the destination to exchange and propagate the logged-in user’s security context when calling the protected CAP service.

Required resources

resources:
  - name: my-application-auth
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: xsuaa
      service-plan: application
      path: ./xs-security.json

  - name: my-application-destination
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: destination
      service-plan: lite
      config:
        HTML5Runtime_enabled: true

  - name: my-application-html5-host
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-host

  - name: my-application-html5-runtime
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-runtime

Connecting the application to SAP Build Work Zone

The SAPUI5 manifest.json should contain the appropriate sap.cloud configuration:

{
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "my.ui5.app",
    "type": "application",
    "applicationVersion": {
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
  },
  "sap.cloud": {
    "public": true,
    "service": "my.application.service"
  }
}

The same sap.cloud.service value must be used consistently in the destination content where applicable.

For example:

sap.cloud.service: my.application.service

I found that a mismatch here could make the deployment succeed while preventing the application from being discovered or resolved correctly in the Work Zone content provider.

After deployment:

  1. Open SAP Build Work Zone administration.
  2. Open the Channel Manager or content provider configuration.
  3. Refresh the HTML5 Apps content provider.
  4. Add the application to My Content.
  5. Assign it to a role.
  6. Add it to a workspace, page, or site.
  7. Ensure the user has the corresponding Work Zone role assignment and XSUAA role collection.

Content Security Policy and VizFrame

After solving the OData routing problem, I encountered another issue: the reports page worked in SAP Build Work Zone, but the charts failed through the standalone approuter.

The browser console displayed an error similar to:

Creating a worker from 'blob:...' violates the following
Content Security Policy directive: "script-src ..."

It also displayed:

Failed to construct 'Worker'

I initially investigated the VizFrame chart configuration because the chart controls were not rendering. However, the chart data and bindings were correct.

The actual problem was that the visualization library attempted to create a web worker using a blob: URL, but the application’s Content Security Policy did not allow it.

I updated the CSP in index.html:

<meta
    http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
    content="
        default-src 'self';
        script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        worker-src 'self' blob:;
        style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        font-src 'self' data:
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        img-src 'self' data: blob:
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        connect-src 'self'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
    "
/>

The important addition was:

worker-src 'self' blob:;

The final CSP should be reviewed according to the organization’s security requirements. Permissions such as 'unsafe-eval' should not be added automatically unless required by the selected SAPUI5 version or application behavior and accepted by the relevant security team.

CSRF protection

The routing examples in this article show:

"csrfProtection": false

This reflects the implementation being discussed, but it should not be interpreted as a recommendation to disable CSRF protection for every route.

For state-changing OData requests, such as:

  • POST
  • PATCH
  • PUT
  • DELETE

the safer approach is to use the OData model’s built-in CSRF handling or explicitly fetch and send a CSRF token.

For example:

X-CSRF-Token: Fetch

The selected approach should be aligned with:

  • The CAP service behavior
  • The SAPUI5 OData model
  • The application’s authentication model
  • Organizational security standards
  • Whether the endpoint is read-only or state-changing

Building and deploying the application

Install the project dependencies:

npm install

Build the CAP project:

npx cds build --production

Build the MTA archive:

mbt build

Log in to the target Cloud Foundry environment:

cf login -a https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Select the correct organization and space:

cf target -o "<organization>" -s "<space>"

Deploy the MTA archive:

cf deploy mta_archives/<archive-name>.mtar

After deployment, verify the application through both entry points.

Standalone approuter

https://<standalone-approuter-route>/

Managed approuter

Open the application through SAP Build Work Zone or the relevant HTML5 application runtime entry point.

Troubleshooting lessons from my implementation

HTTP 404 for OData requests only in SAP Build Work Zone

Symptom

The UI loads, but the OData request returns HTTP 404.

What I initially assumed

I initially treated this as a missing destination or incorrect backend route.

Actual cause

The OData request used a root-relative URL:

/odata/v4/my-service/

This removed the managed-approuter application prefix.

Resolution

Use a component-relative path:

odata/v4/my-service/

and resolve it against the SAPUI5 component location.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized

Possible causes

  • Missing or invalid XSUAA binding
  • Expired authentication session
  • Missing token propagation
  • Destination using the wrong authentication method
  • Direct access to the CAP service instead of access through the approuter

Important lesson

An HTTP 401 response does not always mean the role configuration is wrong. I learned to inspect the complete request URL first.

If the request reached the wrong route because its application prefix was missing, changing scopes or role collections would not solve the problem.

HTTP 403 Forbidden

Possible causes

  • The user is authenticated but lacks the required scope
  • The correct role collection was not assigned
  • The destination propagated a technical token instead of the user token
  • The CAP authorization annotation rejected the user
  • Application-level user provisioning rejected the user

Difference between 401 and 403

A simplified interpretation is:

401: The request does not have acceptable authentication.
403: The identity is known, but it does not have permission.

Application works through Work Zone but not through the standalone approuter

Check the following:

  • Does the standalone approuter contain the built webapp content?
  • Does router/xs-app.json use localDir?
  • Is the standalone approuter bound to XSUAA?
  • Is the srv-api destination injected?
  • Is forwardAuthToken enabled?
  • Is the frontend route placed after the more specific OData routes?

Route order matters because the generic frontend route can otherwise capture requests intended for the backend.

Application works through the standalone approuter but not through Work Zone

Check the following:

  • Was the SAPUI5 ZIP uploaded to the HTML5 Application Repository?
  • Does the HTML5 application contain its own xs-app.json?
  • Is HTML5Runtime_enabled set correctly?
  • Does the destination exist?
  • Does the destination name exactly match srv-api?
  • Is sap.cloud.service consistent?
  • Was the Work Zone content provider refreshed?
  • Was the application assigned to the required role and site?
  • Does the OData URL preserve the managed-approuter application prefix?

Charts fail only in one runtime

Open the browser console and look for:

Content Security Policy

or:

Failed to construct Worker

If VizFrame uses a blob worker, verify that the CSP contains:

worker-src 'self' blob:;

This was particularly instructive because the problem appeared to be in the chart implementation, while the actual cause was browser security policy.

Missing i18n files

SAPUI5 may attempt to load locale-specific files such as:

i18n/i18n_en.properties
i18n/i18n_en_GB.properties

If these files are not available, the browser can display HTTP 404 warnings.

Depending on the application’s localization strategy, either create the required files or verify that the fallback bundle is configured correctly.

Architecture summary

The final architecture I implemented can be summarized as follows:

                           +-------------------------+
                           |       SAP CAP Service   |
                           |     Protected by XSUAA  |
                           +------------+------------+
                                        ^
                                        |
                              User token forwarding
                                        |
                  +---------------------+---------------------+
                  |                                           |
       +----------+-----------+                   +-----------+-----------+
       | Standalone Approuter |                   |   Managed Approuter   |
       | Cloud Foundry App    |                   | SAP Build Work Zone   |
       +----------+-----------+                   +-----------+-----------+
                  |                                           |
       Local SAPUI5 content                       HTML5 App Repository
                  |                                           |
                  +---------------------+---------------------+
                                        |
                              Same SAPUI5 codebase

The two runtimes have different routing responsibilities, but they use the same application logic.

What I would do differently next time

Looking back, I would validate the application through both approuter models much earlier in the development cycle.

My initial local and standalone-approuter testing gave me confidence that the routing was complete. However, it did not expose the managed-approuter prefix behavior.

For a future implementation, I would test these scenarios from the beginning:

  1. Local CAP runtime
  2. Standalone approuter
  3. Managed approuter
  4. Direct OData read
  5. State-changing OData request
  6. Role-restricted request
  7. VizFrame or worker-based UI functionality
  8. Session expiry and reauthentication

I would also inspect the final browser request URL before changing destination or authorization configurations. That simple step would have shortened my troubleshooting considerably.

Key takeaways

The most important lesson from this implementation is that supporting both approuter models is not simply a matter of deploying two routers.

The frontend URL strategy, destination configuration, authentication flow, HTML5 application packaging, and runtime routing must all work together.

My main takeaways were:

  • Do not assume identical-looking URLs behave identically across runtime models.
  • Avoid root-relative service URLs when an application may run behind a managed-approuter prefix.
  • Resolve backend URLs relative to the SAPUI5 component.
  • Keep runtime-specific routing configurations separate.
  • Keep the frontend business logic shared.
  • Forward the authenticated user token to protected CAP services.
  • Do not assume every HTTP 401 or 404 response is caused by XSUAA.
  • Verify the complete browser request URL before changing authorization settings.
  • Ensure sap.cloud.service values are consistent.
  • Treat Content Security Policy as part of the application architecture.
  • Test both runtime models early rather than after the application is complete.

The design allowed me to support direct access and SAP Build Work Zone access using one SAPUI5 codebase and one SAP CAP backend, without hard-coded deployment URLs or duplicated frontend applications.

I hope this experience helps other SAP BTP architects and developers who encounter the same routing and authentication challenges.

I would be interested to hear how others have designed applications that need to support both standalone and managed approuters.

Migrating HTML5 Applications from Neo to Application Frontend Service — Now with AI Skills

SAP Neo is approaching end of life, and if you have HTML5 applications hosted there, you already know you need to move them to the multi-cloud environment. Application Frontend service is the natural destination — it brings back the simplicity and flexibility that Neo developers valued, now built on the multi-cloud foundation.

While SAP Business Application Studio provides a number of tools to assist with migration, the process is still mostly manual.  It can take a few hours for a simple application and up to days for a large-scale application.

We are happy to share a set of AI skills we built to automate most of this work.

Check out these earlier posts for more background about Application Frontend service:

  • Introducing Application Frontend Service
  • Simple UI Applications with Application Frontend Service
  • Moving HTML5 Applications to Application Frontend Service

What Are These AI Skills?

The skill focuses is migration from SAP Neo, but it can also migrate applications based on HTML5 Repository that use a managed approuter or standalone approuter. It targets Cloud Foundry or Kyma runtimes and supports both XSUAA and IAS authentication.

The package ships with three skills, each covering a different phase of the migration lifecycle:

/appfront:migrate analyses your existing HTML5 project, proposes a migration plan, waits for your approval, and then executes all the configuration changes. It never modifies your original project — it copies your original project to a new folder appfront-migrated/ and all changes are done to this copy.

/appfront:validate validates your migrated project configuration for correctness and deployment readiness. It goes through mta.yaml, xs-app.json, xs-security.json, and service bindings, and reports any issues against a known-good checklist. It can also connect to a live deployed application and validate it at runtime.

/appfront:cleanup is used if you want to completely roll back all changes done with the skill. It un-deploys any deployed applications and any related service instances and removes the local output folder. It always asks before any destructive step and never touches your original source project.

The skills are open source and available on GitHub: https://github.com/SAP-samples/html5-applications-migration-skills-for-sap-btp.

What Does the Skill Actually Do?

When you run /appfront:migrate on a Neo HTML5 project, the skill works through the migration in phases:

First, it reads and analyses your source files — neo-app.json, neo-mta.yaml, and manifest.json — and builds a complete picture of your routing, security constraints, and destinations. It then presents you with a migration plan: exactly which files will be created, which will be modified, and which Neo-specific artifacts will be removed. Nothing changes until you approve.

Once you confirm, the skill generates the full Application Frontend configuration:

  • xs-app.json — translated your neo-app.json routes and configurations
  • xs-security.json — Neo security constraints mapped to XSUAA scopes, role templates, and role collections
  • mta.yaml — with a content deployer module for deploying the application resources to Application Frontend

It also updates manifest.json, fixes the UI5 bootstrap path in index.html, and removes Grunt-based build artifacts that are no longer needed.

After generating the files, a built-in critic reviews the output against a checklist to identify common misconfigurations before you deploy.

Note: some steps still require manual action in the BTP cockpit — destination credentials with secrets are not exported from Neo for security reasons, so you will need to add those manually after import.

Note that end-to-end functional testing of your business logic is not included in these estimates. It requires developer or end user involvement and takes the same time regardless of how the technical migration was done.

 Mass Migration

The skills support mass migration of applications. If you have multiple applications with similar characteristics, you can run the skills to migrate all of them in one go. During the process, you can consolidate applications under the same business solution and MTA deployment or keep them completely independent. Simply answer the questions presented by the skill and, if needed, provide instructions in natural language to fine-tune the migration.

 Prerequisites and How to Get It

To use the migration skills, you will need:

  • AI Coding tool like Claude Code installed and connected to an LLM service
  • An SAP BTP subaccount with subscription to Application Frontend service
  • Cloud Foundry CLI  installed and logged in to your target org and space
  • MBT (Cloud MTA Build Tool) installed: npm install -g mbt
  • [Optional] Application Frontend CLI (afctl) installed and logged in for fetching the application URL after deployment: npm install -g @SAP/appfront-cli

Detailed prerequisite list and installation instructions are available in the README file. The skills were built with Claude Code in mind, but they can be installed and used in other coding tools like GitHub Copilot.

Once the skills are installed navigate to your project directory and run /appfront:migrate to get started.

To sum up

If you still have HTML5 applications running in the SAP Neo environment, now is the time to migrate them to SAP multi-cloud. The good news is that, with AI skills like the ones above, the process has become much easier.
Give it a try and let me know in the comments how it worked for you. If you have suggestions for improvement, the best approach would be to contribute them directly to the project’s Git repository.
